title: Cooper Rush struggled, but Falcons' quarterback question is deeper than that The Falcons enter Week 2 with the same question they were asking throughout Week 1: Who is going to start at quarterback? Josh Kendall 14
summary:
Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski hopes to have clarity on the availability of quarterbacks Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. in "the next few days." Justin K. Aller / Getty Images
Kevin Stefanski had plenty to do Monday to sift through the issues from the Atlanta Falcons’ season-opening loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers before turning his attention to the biggest issue of all: Who will start at quarterback for the Falcons in the home opener against the Carolina Panthers this weekend?
“We will see.
full_text:
Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski hopes to have clarity on the availability of quarterbacks Tua Tagovailoa and Michael Penix Jr. in "the next few days." Justin K. Aller / Getty Images
Kevin Stefanski had plenty to do Monday to sift through the issues from the Atlanta Falcons’ season-opening loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers before turning his attention to the biggest issue of all: Who will start at quarterback for the Falcons in the home opener against the Carolina Panthers this weekend?
“We will see. I really don’t have an update yet,” the Falcons’ first-year coach said. “I really need to get through today before we can make that decision.”
The first factor in the decision is health. Tua Tagovailoa was ruled out of the Falcons’ opener because of an oblique injury suffered in Thursday’s practice. Michael Penix Jr. told the coaching staff he still doesn’t feel ready to play while rehabbing the torn ACL that ended his 2025 season, although he said last week he is “really, really close.”
“I hope to have more clarity on all of our positions in regard to injury later today or the next few days,” Stefanski said Monday.
Veteran Cooper Rush started Week 1’s 20-13 loss to the Steelers and went 12-for-22 passing for 143 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions. He posted the worst passer rating (51.9) and air yards per attempt average (3.4) — and the second-worst interception per attempt percentage (9.1 percent) and success rate (34.6 percent) — among starters who completed their games.
“Cooper battled,” Stefanski said Monday, echoing the assessment he provided immediately after Sunday’s loss. “Obviously, you want the turnovers back. You have to give credit to the Steelers, too, but all of our guys can be better.”
The Falcons focused Monday on how to help their quarterback, whoever it’s going to be.
“It’s easy to highlight the quarterback position, but we have to stay on the field,” Stefanski said. “We got in some not great downs and distances for our offense to convert.”
Sunday’s game cost the Falcons Da’Shawn Hand, the veteran defensive tackle who joined the team on a one-year, $3 million free-agent deal this offseason. Hand suffered a quad injury that will require surgery and end his season after just seven snaps.
“It’s hard because of the person that he is,” Stefanski said. “That is the thing I appreciate about him in the first place, just a tough, tough dude. We will look at different things we need to do, but feel really confident in the guys we have in that room. But it’s never easy when you lose a guy like Da’Shawn.”
Atlanta also added Maason Smith and Gervon Dexter to the interior of the defensive line in the offseason, and both played extensively against the Steelers. Dexter played 39 snaps and had three tackles, and Smith played 38 snaps with one pass deflection.
On the other side of the ball, right guard Chris Lindstrom is in the concussion protocol after being injured trying to tackle T.J. Watt on Watt’s interception return.
If you’re thinking the Falcons suffer from some sort of field goal jinx, I’m going to have a hard time proving you wrong. First-year kicker Nick Folk missed three field goal attempts in the three seasons before he arrived in Atlanta (78-of-81), then missed his first two regular-season kicks for the Falcons.
“I take full responsibility for today, bad day on my part,” he said after the game.
Since 2023, no NFL team has lost more points to missed kicks than Atlanta (81), according to TruMedia. Falcons kickers have hit 75.3 percent of their kicks in that span, the second-lowest percentage in the league.
“I will just try to move on and try to learn from it a little bit and go from there,” Folk said.
No kicker in the NFL with more than 20 field goal attempts had a higher success rate than the 41-year-old Folk’s 96.3 percent from 2023 to 2025. He missed from 54 and 45 yards before hitting from 51 and 43 yards in the second half against the Steelers.
“Nick is a pro. I have total faith and trust in Nick,” Stefanski said. “It wasn’t like those were short field goals, at least the first one. He will be better. He will come through for this football team.”
Rookie Zachariah Branch played 18 snaps on offense in his NFL debut but didn’t get a passing target or a carry. He was active in the return game, though, with a 30-yard kick return and three punt returns for 33 yards.
“It was pretty easy,” Branch said. “The guys set up the blocks for me. I just trusted my speed.”
The Falcons ran play-action on only 5.3 percent of their offensive snaps, the lowest percentage in the league in Week 1. Those three snaps resulted in 64 yards, which was 27 percent of their offensive output, and their average of 21.3 yards per play was the highest in the league on play-action in Week 1.
Eighteen Falcons got at least 14 snaps on defense against the Steelers, and maybe the most surprising number on the list was Dexter’s 39, considering he joined the team only two weeks ago.
Rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels started at inside linebacker and played 45 snaps, often being replaced by fellow rookie Harold Perkins Jr. on passing downs. Perkins played 23 snaps.
“With a lot of new guys, we are figuring out roles for them, and I’m proud of the effort,” Stefanski said.
Bijan Robinson touched the ball on 65.9 percent of his 46 snaps, the highest percentage of his career, according to NextGenStats. … Drake London played 59 snaps and got four passing targets and one carry. … The Falcons ran 26 plays with more than one tight end on the field Sunday, the sixth-highest total of the week, according to TruMedia.

title: What's real from NFL Week 1? Breaking down the film on Bengals, 49ers defenses and Ravens, Bills offenses Ted Nguyen 22
summary:

full_text:
The revamped Bengals defensive line, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe (53) and Jonathan Allen (93), showed a massive improvement in dominating a very good Buccaneers offensive line. Jeff Dean / Getty Images
Obviously, Week 1 can be a mirage. Teams that didn’t play their starters in preseason are rusty. The lack of film and information on how teams have changed in the offseason from a schematic and personnel perspective can give some teams an advantage. But it’s not all mirage. Some teams have legitimately improved! Let’s look at units that surprised in Week 1 and decipher how real their improvements are.
The Cincinnati Bengals looked like the perfect defense for an offensive team. On the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ first drive, it looked like defensive coordinator Al Golden wanted to go back to his roots and play heavy man, but they got gashed so he adjusted and went to mostly zone, with some man sprinkled in.
After the first drive, they limited big plays, got takeaways, stiffened up in the red zone and pressured the quarterback. This was a massive improvement for a unit that had some historically bad metrics last season. The Bengals’ revamped defensive line, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe and Jonathan Allen, dominated a very good Buccaneers offensive line for most of the day and had Baker Mayfield scrambling all day. The secondary had a few busts, but they were mostly sticky in man coverage and did a good job of communicating and tackling in zone coverage. Corner DJ Tuner looks like he’s taking that step into the elite tier of corners. He had a play in which he got stiff-armed, rolled back up and made the tackle — usually not a highlight play for a defensive back, but I loved the effort, and it’s an example of the attitude the Bengals defense wants to play with.
Their rush defense looked improved. They aren’t going to shut down the run often, but they didn’t give up explosive runs. Last season, they ranked 31st in rushes of 15+ yards allowed. They didn’t give up any against a Bucs rushing offense that is expected to be explosive.
The Bengals aren’t going to force four turnovers in every game, but they played well against a talented Bucs offense. This looks like a defense that is going to be much better than last year. Even if they regress to a middle of the pack unit, that should be enough to make the Bengals true contenders.
When the Indianapolis Colts defense is healthy, it is a talented group along the defensive line and the outside with two great corners. That being said, the Ravens offense made the Colts look silly. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle’s first game gets a big A+. Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was under center on 41 percent of snaps, which is by far the highest rate in any game of his career. One of Jesse Minter’s best hires was offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford. The Ravens’ revamped offensive line was exceptional blocking outside zone and created phenomenal pass blocking for Jackson, who was rarely bothered and had space to scramble if he needed to. Getting under center helped open the boot game for Jackson, and after the Colts’ defensive ends got tired of Jackson getting to the perimeter, they started sitting outside, which opened huge cutback lanes for Derrick Henry. You can see Ledford’s influence with the running game, as the Ravens repeatedly put a tight end in motion to help with interior double teams, something the Falcons did often last season.
When the scheme didn’t create easy opportunity, Jackson was still Jackson. He can still create second-reaction plays at an elite level. The connectivity he has with Zay Flowers right now is special. There were plays in which the two ad-libbed in sync like Travis Kelce and Patrick Mahomes.
7:10 remaining in the second quarter, second-and-9
Here, Flowers lined up in the backfield to run a choice route. The Colts had a weak-side blitz called, which is a good but aggressive call, knowing Flowers isn’t there to pass block. Safety A.J. Haulcy was supposed to replace No. 57 and essentially match Flowers.
Initially, Flowers settled into the hole in the zone, but Haulcy was running at him with a head of steam. With a free runner coming at him, Jackson had the patience to pump fake Haulcy to get him to jump. Flowers was on the same page and slid inside.
Throwing off-platform, Jackson hit Flowers in stride, and Flowers did the rest, slicing through the defense with electric speed for the touchdown.
BALvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/IQfU8vIXhY
— NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026
The issue with this offense is its lack of receiving talent. Flowers had to leave the game because he injured his hamstring and may miss time. Rookie Ja’Kobi Lane will miss time because of a broken wrist. Doyle’s creativity could get tested early if Flowers can’t play against the New Orleans Saints next week. Still, I am buying stock in this Ravens offense. Right now, I’m buying a lot of stock in this Doyle/Jackson partnership.
In his last two games against the Houston Texans, Josh Allen has struggled mightily. He might have had the best game that I’ve ever seen him play this week. Though the Buffalo Bills aren’t necessarily an improvement candidate because they finished third in points per drive last season, what they did in Reliant Stadium was special. This was the worst game in terms of total defensive EPA per snap for the Texans in three years, and the Bills’ 7.9-yard average per play is the highest that they’ve given up in the time span.
The Bills decided to go big or go home. They weren’t going to play scared and scrapped the traditional run game, handing the ball off only 15 times. Joe Brady smartly didn’t try to “establish the run” before going heavy play action. Forty percent of the Bills’ drop backs were play actions, and Allen took shots downfield. His average air yards per attempt was 13.68, which is the highest against the Texans in the last two years. Brady put together a strong protection plan with physical chips, fake chips and pullers to control the Texans’ dynamic edge rushers.
0:58 remaining in the first quarter, first-and-10
The Bills used this protection scheme frequently on their play-action concepts. On the right side of the line (left of the image), a tight end would chip the end, which would slow him down for left guard Alec Anderson to pull toward him. Left tackle Dion Dawkins was trusted to block Will Anderson one-on-one, but the line would slide in his direction, which gives him some inside presence.
With the line sliding toward his direction, Dawkins could play Anderson heavier on the outside because he could have potential help inside. Center Connor McGovern was occupied here, but he had his eyes on Anderson in case of an inside move and could help as soon as his right guard overtakes his block.
The scheme helped give Allen the time he needed to throw haymakers downfield.
D.J. Moore isn’t an elite receiver, but he’s the best pure separator that Allen has had in a while and gives them an answer against man coverage, which they struggled with last season. A healthy Dalton Kincaid also helps out a ton in that department as well. If elite defenses can’t just man up the Bills offense, look out!
The San Francisco 49ers have declined defensively over the years. They’ve repeatedly tried to stick with their single-high, attacking front scheme, but they simply don’t have the defensive line talent to play that style, which prioritizes keeping things simple so players can play fast. Defensive coordinator Raheem Morris has been a chameleon schematically so it was a bit of mystery of what his defense would look like with the 49ers. What we saw in Australia was the most modern a 49ers defense has looked in a long time.
8:58 remaining in the second quarter, third-and-10
On Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford’s interception on third-and-10, the 49ers initially showed him a man look with a one deep safety.
Stafford assumed he would have one-on-one coverage on Puka Nacua running a corner…

title: Dave Canales has Ejiro Evero's back after Panthers' Week 1 defensive debacle “I like our system. I like our scheme. I’ve seen this scheme work at a high level," Canales said of Evero's defensive system. Joseph Person 18

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — A week into the season, Dave Canales is already defending Ejiro Evero’s scheme Monday after the Carolina Panthers’ defense failed to show for the opener.

full_text:
Caleb Williams had his way with the Carolina defense on the ground and through the air. Bob Donnan / Imagn Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — A week into the season, Dave Canales is already defending Ejiro Evero’s scheme Monday after the Carolina Panthers’ defense failed to show for the opener.
It may have only been one game but it was a doozy for Evero’s defense, which allowed the most points in franchise history in a 59-37 loss to the Chicago Bears that prompted another round of questions about Carolina’s defensive coordinator.
The Panthers wasted a stellar performance by quarterback Bryce Young, whose 361-yard passing day became a footnote after the defense let QB Caleb Williams and the Bears’ backs run roughshod over it.
Chicago rushed for 291 yards and rolled up 552 total yards — both were the third-highest totals by a Carolina opponent — against a defense expected to be improved following the free-agent acquisitions of linebacker Devin Lloyd and edge rusher Jaelan Phillips.
Since 2023 when Evero was hired as Frank Reich’s defensive coordinator, the Panthers have allowed 40 or more points eight times, more than anyone in the league. The Dallas Cowboys have given up 40-plus seven times over that span.
Canales said the Panthers have enough talent to be a successful defense. He also continues to support Evero, who — along with his defensive staff — was retained after Canales was hired in 2024.
“I like our system. I like our scheme. I’ve seen this scheme work at a high level, and I’ve seen us work in this scheme at a high level,” Canales said. “We need to find that week in and week out. All of us are disappointed with how it played out, but this is the work we have.”
This is the second time in three years that the Panthers’ defense has had a rough Week 1. The New Orleans Saints blew out Carolina 47-10 in Canales’ first game in 2024. The Derek Carr-led Saints finished with 379 yards, a drop in the bucket compared to what Bears coach Ben Johnson and Williams were able to do Sunday.
“Players and coaches alike gotta be better,” defensive lineman Bobby Brown said Monday. “Players didn’t execute all the time. Coach E already told us he didn’t get us in the best call all the time.”
Canales thought the defense played hard but not smart against the Bears, a sentiment shared by defensive tackle Derrick Brown, who took responsibility for his two penalties that led directly to 14 points for the Bears.
Evero’s scheme relies heavily on two-high safeties and disguised coverages meant to confuse quarterbacks as they look for pre-snap tells. But against the run, the front seven has to be disciplined in its gaps because of the deep alignment of the safeties.
Chicago had several running plays where its backs reached the second level of the defense untouched and with a full head of steam. The most glaring example came on Kyle Monangai’s 61-yard touchdown run, when he burst into an open hole and eluded the diving tackle attempts of safety Nick Scott and Chau Smith-Wade.
“The way that we employ the safeties, the way we move our secondary around, it keeps offenses guessing,” Canales said. “It does put pressure on the front and the safeties show up from depth to fit into the gaps. But we’ve gotta be really connected on that front seven to make sure that a lot of the runs are getting bottlenecked into alleys and our guys can show up.”
Compounding matters was the Panthers’ inability to keep Williams in the pocket, which has been a chore for nearly every team that’s faced him. Outside linebacker Princely Umanmielen, who started in place of the injured Pat Jones, lost containment on Williams’ 9-yard touchdown in the first quarter, the first of two scoring scrambles for the No. 1 pick from 2024.
“I think I rushed pretty well,” said Umanmielen, who had one of the Panthers’ two sacks on Williams. “Some of those I plays I had (where) I pushed the pocket pretty well, I would say I pushed it great. But a quarterback like Caleb Williams, it’s hard. He’s very athletic. He’s very gifted. A lot of other quarterbacks in the NFL wouldn’t have made those type of plays.”
Evero last week said Williams has “magic to him,” almost like a “sixth sense” for knowing when pass rushers are around him. That proved prophetic when Williams time and again escaped danger and extended plays, rushing 10 times for 65 yards and the two TDs.
Bobby Brown, who had an interception negated by an offsides penalty on Derrick Brown, said the Panthers could have been better staying in their rush lanes.
“He made the plays that he should have made, that he’s good at making, that he’s known for making,” Brown said. “But we also gave him a few.”
Evero’s two-high shell look is designed to limit explosive plays. But Williams’ second TD run — a 29-yarder — was one of eight plays for Chicago of at least 22 yards. Three of the Bears’ four longest plays were runs.
Canales said the guys up front can’t let backs get through the first line of defense unimpeded.
“When you look at those point-of-attack plays that safeties have or that corners have out in space, out in the field, all of a sudden it’s an open-field tackling drill,” he said. “We’re not fitting things up, and we don’t make the backs check their feet and have to bounce something or slow down so we can all get there in a timely fashion. That all starts up front. That all starts with the proper fit.”
Brown, who played for the Los Angeles Rams when Evero was an assistant coach, agreed that the front four could have been more disruptive. “When I was at L.A., the biggest thing was we lived in the backfield,” he said. “I don’t think we was in the backfield at all yesterday. I don’t know if we had too many (tackles for loss) other than sacks.”
Besides the sacks, linebacker Bobby Okereke and outside linebacker Trevis Gipson had the Panthers’ only other TFLs.
The defense will look to get healthy this week against the Atlanta Falcons, who started journeyman quarterback Cooper Rush on Sunday after Tua Tagovailoa injured his oblique and Michael Penix continued his recovery from ACL surgery.
Rush threw two interceptions in a 20-13 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers, including one that T.J. Watt returned for a touchdown. Rush’s 51.9 quarterback rating was the worst among all Week 1 starters.
It’s unclear who will start at QB for the Falcons this week. Whoever it is, it’s hard to imagine him playing better than Williams did Sunday. If that happens, the Panthers have a big problem.
While no one liked the result, Umanmielen said seeing Williams early should help the Panthers in the long run.
“Like we have Lamar Jackson coming up (in November),” he said. “I think having this challenge Week 1 is really gonna help us going into how we play these next quarterbacks these upcoming games.”

title: 'Keep scoring points': How the Bears offense developed its relentless mindset Think the Bears' 59-point eruption at Carolina was an anomaly? Ben Johnson and company have aspirations for so much more. Dan Wiederer 19

Early last offseason, even with a long list of concerns and desired improvement areas, Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson gave his offense a target. Wayyyy off in the distance, mind you. In a stratosphere folks in Chicago have only heard about — and still aren’t sure really exists.

full_text:
Bears tight end Cole Kmet says, "I don't think there's anybody in the league we should be afraid to go against defensively." Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
Early last offseason, even with a long list of concerns and desired improvement areas, Chicago Bears coach Ben Johnson gave his offense a target. Wayyyy off in the distance, mind you. In a stratosphere folks in Chicago have only heard about — and still aren’t sure really exists.
Still, this is the wiring of a relentlessly driven leader who is praised by his assistant coaches for what offensive coordinator Press Taylor called his “unique desire to achieve.”
Thus, after helping the Bears leap to ninth in the NFL in scoring last season (25.9 points per game) from 28th in 2024 (18.2 ppg), Johnson had zero hesitation invoking the 2013 Denver Broncos.
The Peyton Manning-led Broncos. The group that rampaged through the regular season for 606 points over 16 games, an average of 37.9. An NFL record.
That , Johnson told his players, is what we are striving to top.
To the casual observer, that might sound ridiculous or quixotic. And you can imagine how a challenge like that might have first hit even with an insider like tight end Cole Kmet, who for his first five seasons as a Bear had never been part of an offense that averaged even 24 points per game. But when asked about Johnson’s target during the first week of training camp, Kmet lit up.
“We want to score a lot of points, and we want to be unforgiving about it,” he said. “I think we definitely have that potential.”
The formula, Kmet had noticed, was already coming together nicely. The Bears had a surplus of talent mixed with versatility combined with attention to detail — all under the oversight of an offensive visionary in Johnson and put into the hands of a gifted quarterback in Caleb Williams.
“I don’t think there’s anybody in the league we should be afraid to go against defensively,” Kmet said. “We’ve got all the guys we need for this season.”
Almost immediately, the challenge Johnson issued resonated with players exactly how he hoped. It was less about the goal itself and much more about the mentality that needed to crystallize to chase it.
Maximum effort, full focus and collective buy-in were required. And after the Bears exploded for 59 points and 552 total yards in Sunday’s season-opening road win against the Carolina Panthers, it sure was notable how many offensive players were convinced they were nowhere near their peak.
“It’s amazing to come out of a game like that and still have so much to clean up,” running back D’Andre Swift said.
Added Darnell Wright: “We left some things out there for sure.”
For what it’s worth, the 2013 Broncos opened their season with a similar explosion — 510 yards and 49 points in a primetime thumping of the reigning Super Bowl champion Baltimore Ravens. Bears running backs coach Eric Studesville was there that night, on John Fox’s staff in Denver and overseeing a running backs room that included Knowshon Moreno, Montee Ball and Ronnie Hillman. But it was Manning who was lighting off the fireworks.
“I think he threw five or six touchdowns in that game to start us out,” Studesville said.
To be fair, it’s easy to lose count. Manning delivered seven touchdown passes over the final three quarters of that win. Wide receivers Demaryius Thomas and Wes Welker and tight end Julius Thomas all scored twice and receiver Andre Caldwell had a TD of his own.
The Broncos were a wagon that season, topping 40 points six times and cracking 50 three times. They averaged 457.3 yards per game and earned the AFC’s top seed, with Manning setting NFL records for passing yards (5,477) and touchdown passes (55) while winning league MVP honors.
Studesville, though, wants it known that it was not a one-man show.
“The offense we produced that year was because a bunch of guys came together and were together to do that,” he said. “There are some names in there that get a lot of credit for it individually. And they should.
“But that was a group of guys who came to work every day and did everything they could to give that team the best chance to win.”
That’s an important footnote Bears coaches keep pounding home. Collective investment is non-negotiable in this pursuit of excellence.
The front office and coaching staff have worked together to assemble a group of players with palpable hunger and elite work habits. And the players have responded by pouring into the demands of their Type-A head coach.
Perhaps it was fitting then, on Sunday, when Swift, two days after landing a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension and then rushing for 124 yards and three touchdowns, accepted his game ball inside the visiting locker room of Bank of America Stadium and pushed his teammates to dive right back into the grind.
“We work too hard, fellas,” Swift said. “Let that work show week in and week out.”
For these Bears, so much of this is about attitude and understanding where the results originate. Under Johnson’s guidance, this group continues to immerse itself in its preparation.
When production like Sunday’s follows, the positive reinforcement grows exponentially.
Guard Jonah Jackson accepted a game ball Sunday on behalf of the offensive line after it paved the way for a bruising 291-yard rushing day, the Bears’ best effort as a franchise since September 1984.
“We were firing on all cylinders,” Jackson said. “And there’s still some meat left on the bone for us.”
And Williams? After accounting for 334 total yards and four touchdowns? He had this to say.
“This is going to be our worst game,” Williams said. “I know the points won’t necessarily show that. But with execution, with blocking, with holding penalties and all these different things, it’s being able to be a truther about who we are and go watch the film.”
One of the more significant moments from the weekend, Johnson noted, came during the final quarterbacks meeting Saturday night in Charlotte, N.C. After a week of being flooded with opponent-specific intel and game plan information, Williams’ preparation was obvious.
“He was on top of it,” Johnson said. “Everything he was rattling off. ‘Where my eyes need to be, what I’m thinking…’ It was bop-bop-bop-bop-bop. I went to bed, and I slept really well.”
Kmet’s combination of delight, amusement and satisfaction was also evident inside a revved-up Bears locker room.
“That was wild. … This is kind of a different thing to be a part of,” he said.
Still, by now players understand well that the kind of excitement Sunday’s offensive eruption produced — with talking heads leaguewide now debating the Bears’ ultimate potential — must also be accompanied by an acknowledgment that the clean-up process for Week 2 will be demanding.
Again, the results were nice and all — 552 yards, 26 first downs, eight touchdowns, 59 points. But Kmet and his offensive teammates anticipated plenty of blemishes in the video review.
That list goes on, too, requiring sober eyes for the in-house evaluation.
Said Kmet: “When you look at the film, you just take it play to play. You’re not really concerned about the scoreboard. Win or loss, you’re looking at the film for what it is from an objective stance. There are going to be plays that we really liked and look great. And then there are going to be plays that we need to fix.”
All that messiness Sunday and still 59 points?
And even after running back Kyle Monangai broke loose for a 61-yard touchdown run to put the Bears ahead by 14 points late in the third quarter, the offense knew its mission.
Remember that edict from the top about being unforgiving?
“It’s just keep scoring points until they tell you to stop,” Kmet said last month. “We’re trying to score every time we have the ball in our hands.”
Imagine Johnson’s delight when the Bears finished Sunday with touchdown drives of 61 and 49 yards, a closing statement on an attention-grabbing day.
Their final possession began with 4:00 left, a 15-point lead and a goal of finishing with the ball in…

full_text:
Devin Singletary and the Giants surprised the favored Cowboys behind a strong all-around performance on Sunday night. Elsa / Getty Images
Every week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
Week 1 was a doozy! The best team in the league — a “superteam,” or so we thought based on our initial power rankings — got hammered, a Super Bowl rematch didn’t change the result from February, at least three Super Bowl contenders opened with a loss and points were way up .
With that, the first week of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, and we finally have some meaningful results to examine. So let’s take a look in this week’s power rankings at what we learned from each team.
What we learned: The offense is still humming
After the franchise’s drama-filled offseason and with questions about the aging roster, the 49ers had no trouble moving the ball against the Rams. Brock Purdy threw for three touchdowns, the running game (including rookie Kaelon Black) looked good and Raheem Morris’ defense was great. It’d be hard to draw up a better start.
Up next: vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Beat Patriots 13-10
What we learned: That run defense is still elite
Against a Patriots team that spent its whole offseason focused on running the ball better after getting humiliated in the Super Bowl, the Seahawks’ run defense dominated once again. Seattle limited New England to 2.5 yards per attempt on its designed rushes. Plenty is still unknown about how long Sam Darnold will be out, but — no surprise — the defense is still great.
Up next: at Cardinals, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
What we learned: They’re the AFC favorites
The Bills were a trendy pick to reach the Super Bowl this season, even in their first year under new coach Joe Brady. They showed why on Sunday. The Texans might have the best defense in the NFL, yet the Bills put up 409 yards of offense while Josh Allen threw for a pair of touchdowns and added another two on the ground. That offense will be fun for the home crowd to watch as Buffalo unveils its new stadium Thursday night.
Up next: vs. Lions, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
1-0. pic.twitter.com/XguSOY6RL8
— Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 13, 2026
Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37
What we learned: Best offense in the NFL?
Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
What we learned: The young OC might work
The Ravens raised some eyebrows around the league during the offseason when they hired a 29-year-old offensive coordinator. Declan Doyle is now 30, but the young coach and a healthy Lamar Jackson led to an impressive rout in Week 1 that featured 506 yards of offense.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Thursday: Lost to 49ers 27-7
What we learned: Sleep helps
The season didn’t start well for the NFL’s superteam that has Super Bowl-or-bust aspirations. Matthew Stafford, the defending league MVP, threw for just 155 yards with no touchdowns and an interception in Australia. Now Myles Garrett is on injured reserve and out for at least four games.
Up next: vs. Giants, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Monday: Beat Broncos 31-10
What we learned: They have a running game!
After dealing with an inconsistent ground attack last season, the Chiefs went out and signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III. It took Walker one game to make a big impact. All eyes in the opener were on Patrick Mahomes’ return, but it was Walker who stole the show, totaling 191 yards of offense and two touchdowns, and adding a new dimension to the K.C. offense.
Up next: vs. Colts, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Saints 31-30 (OT)
What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble
The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown.
Up next: at Bills, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Bills 36-31
What we learned: The defense is beatable
That side of the ball is supposed to carry this team. Even though the Bills had the ball for under 24 minutes of game time, the Texans’ usually dominant defense still got gashed at home. C.J. Stroud was better Sunday than in the playoffs, which is the last time we saw him, but his strip-sack in the final seconds cemented Houston’s loss.
Up next: vs. Bengals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Lost to Seahawks 13-10
What we learned: Drake Maye’s slump isn’t over
The Patriots had hoped that Maye’s four-game postseason slide last season was largely the result of a shoulder injury and some big games in bad weather against great defenses. But with a full offseason to prepare, Maye struggled again against the Seahawks, throwing three interceptions, including a brutal one in the end zone when New England easily could’ve forced overtime.
Up next: vs. Steelers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Commanders 24-22
What we learned: Jalen Hurts can still produce moments
The final box score isn’t going to instill a ton of faith that the Eagles’ offense has suddenly morphed back into one of the league’s best. But Hurts made enough big plays when his team needed him, connecting on a deep ball and improvising with his legs on a third-and-18 conversion to offer hope as Philadelphia settles into this new offensive scheme under Sean Mannion.
Up next: at Titans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Monday: Lost to Chiefs 31-10
What we learned: There’s concern on offense
In a bit of a surprise this offseason, coach Sean Payton relinquished offensive play-calling duties to 31-year-old coordinator Davis Webb. His debut didn’t go well. After a pair of offseason ankle surgeries, Bo Nix fumbled three times, threw an interception and managed just 4.7 yards per attempt, while new receiver Jaylen Waddle had only one catch for 2 yards.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Did we really learn anything about the Jaguars by watching them beat a hapless Browns team? Still, props to them for jumping out to a 31-0 lead and putting it on cruise control behind a great game from Trevor Lawrence and an impressive showing from the defense. Now, the schedule turns brutal with five straight games against teams with Super Bowl hopes.
Up next: at Broncos, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Buccaneers 33-27
What we learned: They have a defense!
The bar might have been on the floor for that side of the ball after last season, but the new-look Cincinnati defense came to play against Tampa Bay, forcing four turnovers and notching four sacks. It was an especially impressive win considering Ja’Marr Chase caught only two passes for 12 yards.
Up next: at Texans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 39-22
What we learned: Brian Flores is a mad man
And we mean that in a good way. The Minnesota defensive coordinator sent blitzes on 74 percent(!) of the Packers’ dropbacks and totally overwhelmed their offensive line late as the Vikings put together an impressive comeback win with backup quarterback Carson Wentz leading the offense.
Up next: at Bears, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 20-13
What we learned: Things look familiar
Yes, the Steelers have a new coach, but this team looked much like it has in recent years. The defense was pretty good. The offense was mostly fine. It’s rarely worth putting too much stock into Week 1, but this Mike McCarthy-led squad looks like another roughly .500 team. We should learn more about the Steelers in Week 2 during their trip to New England.
Up next: at Patriots, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 39-22
What we learned: New season, same Packers
That was the headline…

title: How Bengals view LBs Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr.'s 2026 debuts The second-year linebackers were much maligned as rookies, but showed promise in Sunday's win over the Buccaneers. Paul Dehner Jr. 12
summary:

CINCINNATI — Midway through Monday’s position meeting, Bengals linebackers coach Mike Hodges decided to pause the tape breakdown of Sunday’s 33-27 win against Tampa Bay to make one point clear to his group.

full_text:
Demetrius Knight Jr. celebrates after the Bengals' win over the Buccaneers on Sunday. Jeff Dean / Getty Images
CINCINNATI — Midway through Monday’s position meeting, Bengals linebackers coach Mike Hodges decided to pause the tape breakdown of Sunday’s 33-27 win against Tampa Bay to make one point clear to his group.
“I actually had to stop the meeting today and make sure that they knew I was proud of them and that we did actually win the game,” Hodges said. “Because I was pretty hard on them and I felt like every play I was critiquing, critiquing, critiquing.”
Second-year starters Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr. didn’t budge at the harsh feedback. Quite the opposite, actually.
“The greatest thing about this room and why I appreciate them so much, they look at me like, ‘You’re good, we know why you are doing this because we can elevate this thing,'” Hodges said.
They’re also used to hearing about the negative. Carter and Knight were at the center of last year’s defensive disaster, playing next to each other as rookies and having to come to grips with ranking as the NFL’s lowest-graded linebackers.
They emerged from the darkness into the 88-degree sunlight at Paycor Stadium on Sunday and were at the center of the game’s biggest plays and all over the stat sheet.
It wasn’t perfect. Far from it, as Hodges spent most of the afternoon ensuring those in his room knew. Yet, if they needed any proof of how he felt, they could just count how many times he leapt in the air while running up and down the sideline following Carter’s half-sack that led to Knight’s scoop-and-score for the first touchdown of the season.
“It was fun, it was so exciting,” Hodges said. “You’re happy for your players to have that.”
The play provided a fitting microcosm of their day and where they are developmentally. Carter did a fantastic job working off the block to get his hands on Baker Mayfield before Myles Murphy finished him off. However, Carter wasn’t supposed to be blitzing in the first place.
“There were some things that were not how you draw them up in the playbook, boys,” Hodges said. “Sometimes it’s good to be a little more lucky and fall into things.”
Taking advantage of falling into things still mattered. In many ways, they provided proof of concept.
Carter’s confidence hasn’t wavered despite criticism following his rookie season. That’s a major reason he still wears the green dot and is kept in charge of the operation of the defense.
“That’s a play that, quite frankly, being honest, we expect to make that,” Carter said. “I mean that in the most humble way possible. We work toward scoring defensive touchdowns. It’s just step one in the journey. There’s still a lot more plays to be made. A lot of plays left out there we need to make, but the Bengals are 1-0, that’s all we can ask for.”
The organization spent the offseason defending the decision not to sign any real competition or spend a draft pick on the position. De facto general manager Duke Tobin defended his belief in them after the draft. Defensive coordinator Al Golden said other coaches around the league would love to have his situation with two 100-tackle linebackers returning.
One of the biggest decisions of the 2025 season for coach Zac Taylor was benching Logan Wilson in favor of Carter last year in Week 5. He did so with the belief those reps would make his defense better for the long haul.
Sunday started to pay that off. Knight posted seven tackles and the scoop-and-score. Carter totaled eight tackles, a half-sack, a forced fumble and a tackle for loss.
“I told Barrett he should have had 11 tackles, a half-sack and forced fumble and he didn’t,” Hodges said. “Some of that was technical and fundamentals.”
Both things can be true. There’s reason to believe in Knight and Carter’s progress in the 2026 debut and also reason to understand there are still areas of concern.
Missed tackles head that list.
Carter and Knight each posted three missed tackles, according to Pro Football Focus. Those were tied for the second-most among all linebackers over the weekend.
Carter only had four missed tackles over the final seven games of last season as he seemed to take a positive step. Knight posted the same numbers over that stretch.
To start with three each provided a critical footnote in an otherwise productive day. The Bengals as a whole missed 14 tackles after averaging 9.6 missed tackles per game last season.
Golden didn’t set off any alarms on the matter, specifically considering Tampa Bay running back Bucky Irving led the NFL in missed tackles forced two years ago.
“I am encouraged by the tackling,” he said. “Number one, I think Bucky is as elusive lateral step as there is … there are a lot of good players in this league. You have to give them credit. You can’t be perfect, but I thought we were physical. We ran to the ball, we populated the ball so it was on the ground and we got it.”
Week 1 will bring missed tackles. Inevitably, that’s life in an NFL with minimal contact or preseason playing time for the starters. The more encouragement stemmed from willingness.
“There’s gonna be moments where we got to do better, come to balance and get guys to the ground,” Taylor said. “But I thought the effort was there. I thought guys did a good job of leveraging the ball. I thought our vice tackling, you saw a lot of jerseys around the ball.”
The occasional missed tackle is easier to swallow when surrounded by impact plays. That’s the difference right now. With Dexter Lawrence and the block-absorbing defensive line in front of them, Carter and Knight largely made the plays that came to them — or they “fell into.”
Hodges credits Carter’s instincts, which showed when he sniffed out a screen to Irving for a tackle for loss and chased through the trash to the sideline to track down a wide run.
“Demetrius played fast,” Golden said. “I think Barrett had some really nice plays. The play on the screen was really, really good. Had some nice run fits, and his overall command was really good with the green dot.”
That was basically the theme of their 2026 debut. They looked like the confident players the Bengals wanted to see in Year 2.
“They trust the talent around them,” Taylor said. “So you don’t have to do too much. I thought that they had really good command of the defense. Barrett, with the headset, and doing a good job getting us in the right calls. So I was impressed. And again, there’s improvement for everybody we had, but I thought it was a good starting point.”

title: What's real from NFL Week 1? Breaking down the film on Bengals, 49ers defenses and Ravens, Bills offenses Ted Nguyen 22

Obviously, Week 1 can be a mirage. Teams that didn’t play their starters in preseason are rusty. The lack of film and information on how teams have changed in the offseason from a schematic and personnel perspective can give some teams an advantage. But it’s not all mirage. Some teams have leg
full_text:
The revamped Bengals defensive line, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe (53) and Jonathan Allen (93), showed a massive improvement in dominating a very good Buccaneers offensive line. Jeff Dean / Getty Images
Obviously, Week 1 can be a mirage. Teams that didn’t play their starters in preseason are rusty. The lack of film and information on how teams have changed in the offseason from a schematic and personnel perspective can give some teams an advantage. But it’s not all mirage. Some teams have legitimately improved! Let’s look at units that surprised in Week 1 and decipher how real their improvements are.
The Cincinnati Bengals looked like the perfect defense for an offensive team. On the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ first drive, it looked like defensive coordinator Al Golden wanted to go back to his roots and play heavy man, but they got gashed so he adjusted and went to mostly zone, with some man sprinkled in.
After the first drive, they limited big plays, got takeaways, stiffened up in the red zone and pressured the quarterback. This was a massive improvement for a unit that had some historically bad metrics last season. The Bengals’ revamped defensive line, with Dexter Lawrence, Boye Mafe and Jonathan Allen, dominated a very good Buccaneers offensive line for most of the day and had Baker Mayfield scrambling all day. The secondary had a few busts, but they were mostly sticky in man coverage and did a good job of communicating and tackling in zone coverage. Corner DJ Tuner looks like he’s taking that step into the elite tier of corners. He had a play in which he got stiff-armed, rolled back up and made the tackle — usually not a highlight play for a defensive back, but I loved the effort, and it’s an example of the attitude the Bengals defense wants to play with.
Their rush defense looked improved. They aren’t going to shut down the run often, but they didn’t give up explosive runs. Last season, they ranked 31st in rushes of 15+ yards allowed. They didn’t give up any against a Bucs rushing offense that is expected to be explosive.
The Bengals aren’t going to force four turnovers in every game, but they played well against a talented Bucs offense. This looks like a defense that is going to be much better than last year. Even if they regress to a middle of the pack unit, that should be enough to make the Bengals true contenders.
When the Indianapolis Colts defense is healthy, it is a talented group along the defensive line and the outside with two great corners. That being said, the Ravens offense made the Colts look silly. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle’s first game gets a big A+. Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was under center on 41 percent of snaps, which is by far the highest rate in any game of his career. One of Jesse Minter’s best hires was offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford. The Ravens’ revamped offensive line was exceptional blocking outside zone and created phenomenal pass blocking for Jackson, who was rarely bothered and had space to scramble if he needed to. Getting under center helped open the boot game for Jackson, and after the Colts’ defensive ends got tired of Jackson getting to the perimeter, they started sitting outside, which opened huge cutback lanes for Derrick Henry. You can see Ledford’s influence with the running game, as the Ravens repeatedly put a tight end in motion to help with interior double teams, something the Falcons did often last season.
When the scheme didn’t create easy opportunity, Jackson was still Jackson. He can still create second-reaction plays at an elite level. The connectivity he has with Zay Flowers right now is special. There were plays in which the two ad-libbed in sync like Travis Kelce and Patrick Mahomes.
7:10 remaining in the second quarter, second-and-9
Here, Flowers lined up in the backfield to run a choice route. The Colts had a weak-side blitz called, which is a good but aggressive call, knowing Flowers isn’t there to pass block. Safety A.J. Haulcy was supposed to replace No. 57 and essentially match Flowers.
Initially, Flowers settled into the hole in the zone, but Haulcy was running at him with a head of steam. With a free runner coming at him, Jackson had the patience to pump fake Haulcy to get him to jump. Flowers was on the same page and slid inside.
Throwing off-platform, Jackson hit Flowers in stride, and Flowers did the rest, slicing through the defense with electric speed for the touchdown.
BALvsIND on CBS/Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/IQfU8vIXhY
— NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026
The issue with this offense is its lack of receiving talent. Flowers had to leave the game because he injured his hamstring and may miss time. Rookie Ja’Kobi Lane will miss time because of a broken wrist. Doyle’s creativity could get tested early if Flowers can’t play against the New Orleans Saints next week. Still, I am buying stock in this Ravens offense. Right now, I’m buying a lot of stock in this Doyle/Jackson partnership.
In his last two games against the Houston Texans, Josh Allen has struggled mightily. He might have had the best game that I’ve ever seen him play this week. Though the Buffalo Bills aren’t necessarily an improvement candidate because they finished third in points per drive last season, what they did in Reliant Stadium was special. This was the worst game in terms of total defensive EPA per snap for the Texans in three years, and the Bills’ 7.9-yard average per play is the highest that they’ve given up in the time span.
The Bills decided to go big or go home. They weren’t going to play scared and scrapped the traditional run game, handing the ball off only 15 times. Joe Brady smartly didn’t try to “establish the run” before going heavy play action. Forty percent of the Bills’ drop backs were play actions, and Allen took shots downfield. His average air yards per attempt was 13.68, which is the highest against the Texans in the last two years. Brady put together a strong protection plan with physical chips, fake chips and pullers to control the Texans’ dynamic edge rushers.
0:58 remaining in the first quarter, first-and-10
The Bills used this protection scheme frequently on their play-action concepts. full_text:
The Cowboys were chasing Giants QB Jaxson Dart all night Sunday. Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images
No one would argue that the Dallas Cowboys have as much talent on defense as they do on offense. Their biggest offseason additions were all on the defensive side of the ball, including their first three draft picks. They would probably need another similar offseason to bridge that gap.
But many of the Cowboys’ biggest defensive issues in their 28-20 season-opening loss to the New York Giants on Sunday night were not about talent. And that’s concerning with all of the offseason defensive coaching staff changes.
Communication and discipline were the team’s two biggest defensive issues, according to Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer.
After watching the game film, Schottenheimer saw too many examples of poor communication either being delivered or received. It led to too many big plays that prevented Dallas from getting off the field. The Cowboys only had two possessions in the entire second half.
The discipline issues came while attempting to keep contain against New York quarterback Jaxson Dart . He finished with 11 carries for 54 yards, including one for 22. The Cowboys face Washington’s Jayden Daniels on Sunday and then Baltimore’s Lamar Jackson the following week. If those problems continue, it’s a decent bet Dallas starts the season 0-3.
“It’s part of the learning curve,” Schottenheimer said Monday. “We have to get better, but we’re going to make mistakes. I see this defense every day and we did not perform well enough as a football team last night, coaching and playing. It’s certainly not the standard. But I’m also not ready to say the expectations for where we think we’re going to get to as a defense and as a football team are not accurate.”
Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones said Monday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas that they “probably had a little unrealistic expectations” in terms of what they could immediately do defensively with all the new coaches and players added in the offseason.
The Cowboys didn’t play many of their starters in the preseason by design. They wanted to get to Week 1 as healthy as possible. And they accomplished that goal. Starting inside linebacker DeMarvion Overshown and starting safety Malik Hooker exited Sunday night’s game with injuries, but the Cowboys were basically at full health defensively entering the game.
Schottenheimer doesn’t second-guess that plan.
“It’s a philosophy and it’s a catch-22,” he said. “If you put a player out there and all of a sudden someone comes and they get dinged up and they’re out for the year, you’re damned if you do, you’re damned if you don’t. I felt really, really good about our work in training camp. I felt really good about the work in the two (practices with the Los Angeles Rams and New Orleans Saints).
“There was plenty of padded work. We just did not perform to the level that we should perform to (Sunday) night and we own that. I’m always going to be the first one off the bus taking responsibility and accountability for that. We’ll get back to work. We got the right guys in this locker room to fix it.”
There’s only so much that can be gleaned from watching training camp practices. The players aren’t tackling to the ground, and the quarterbacks can’t even be touched. Maybe most important of all, the offense isn’t going to stick with certain plays just because it’s working. Both sides are trying to get as much work for their side of the ball. It’s not like a game where an opponent will continue running something because the other side is showing it can’t stop them. That was on display in Dallas’ loss to the Giants.
According to Pro Football Focus’ individual player grading, Dallas’ top five defenders against the Giants were outside linebacker Donovan Ezeiruaku, defensive linemen Otito Ogbonnia and Quinnen Williams, rookie defensive back Caleb Downs and cornerback Cobie Durant.
The most notable of the Cowboys’ lowest-graded defensive players, according to PFF, were Overshown, inside linebacker Dee Winters, rookie outside linebacker Malachi Lawrence, Hooker, outside linebacker Rashan Gary, safety Jalen Thompson and outside linebacker Von Miller.
One poor showing won’t mean much if the issues are corrected in the coming weeks. A noticeable jump should come from Week 1 to Week 2 for a team playing so many new players who are working with a new coaching staff. Much of that responsibility falls on the shoulders of new defensive coordinator Christian Parker.
Schottenheimer said the two had great discussions after the game and again Monday morning at the team’s headquarters. Nothing that happened Sunday night has changed the way the second-year head coach feels about the first-time defensive coordinator.
“He’s been great,” Schottenheimer said. “Very methodical, as you would imagine, just like what we’ve seen with every experience and exposure to him. Very methodical, very convicted. Didn’t make excuses. ‘Need to be better. Will be better, starting with X, Y, Z.’
“He and I were on the same page with that, which is a good thing. And then this morning he was amazing with the staff and having hard conversations and real conversations. And this is not just the players, this is us as a staff. That’s a leader. That’s a leader of men.”
Things can’t go much worse than they did a year ago for Dallas’ defense. It was arguably the worst in franchise history. It was so bad that Matt Eberflus didn’t get a second season as defensive coordinator. Some of those issues looked to still be hanging around Sunday night.
Schottenheimer has confidence Parker will fix them.
“I’m around him every day,” Schottenheimer said. “There’s adversity all the time in what we do. You (reporters) don’t hear about all of it. You don’t see all of it. You don’t deal with all of it. But whether it’s the things we deal with off the field, whether it’s the things we deal with in coaching meetings and discussions that we have from a strategy standpoint, from a personnel standpoint, and until you go through all those things, you don’t really know.
“But I have no question Christian Parker is the right guy for this job. He’s an outstanding coach. He will learn from this, just like our young players are going to learn from this. We’re going to play our young players this weekend, too. They’re going to play better and Christian’s going to call a better game this week and feel better about it.”

full_text:
A season of sky-high expectations opened with a flop for Bo Nix and the Denver offense. Denny Medley / Imagn Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Bo Nix pulled his back off the Arrowhead Stadium grass and stared into a sea of red-clad fans roaring in delight at his demise.
Nix sat there for just a moment, as if he was in disbelief after fumbling for the third time and being sacked for the fourth in Monday night’s 31-10, season-opening loss to the Chiefs.
How could a return to action he had anticipated for so long go so poorly?
“Pretty pitiful, actually,” Nix said.
Perhaps the only solace for the Broncos after a season of sky-high expectations opened with a flop is those sorts of sad adjectives belonged to everyone. Misery had plenty of company. Nix, in his first game since he had two offseason ankle injuries, was sacked on the game’s first play. He threw an interception on his first pass attempt. There were dropped passes and ill-timed penalties. The Broncos missed 28 tackles, according to Next Gen Stats. Not even their infamous 70-20 loss in Miami three years ago, three games into Vance Joseph’s return to Denver as defensive coordinator, featured that many whiffs. The Broncos were pushed around and outclassed by a Kansas City team that sent a clear message: The Chiefs want their AFC West crown, the one the Broncos ripped away last season to snap a nine-year run by the red-and-gold, back.
“They came in here and they whooped our butt,” safety Talanoa Hufanga said.
A Week 1 result can’t sink a season. But it can increase pressure and scrutiny. That will be especially true for new offensive coordinator Davis Webb after the Broncos’ offense sputtered in ways big and small Monday night.
Webb, after receiving the play-calling baton from head coach Sean Payton in the spring, represented one of the only major changes for Denver this offseason, a bright young coach put into the role to help Nix and the offense reach another level. That could very well prove to be the case, but it wasn’t in the opener. The Broncos went a combined 2 of 13 on third and fourth downs. Most of the team’s seven penalties came on the offensive side of the ball, including a handful that wiped out scoring opportunities. Denver did not produce a single play of at least 20 yards and averaged only 4.7 yards per pass attempt. The Broncos’ big offseason addition, wide receiver Jaylen Waddle? He had one catch for 2 yards.
On a weekend in the NFL that featured record scoring numbers across the league, the Broncos mustered their lowest scoring output in a regular-season road game since at 41-10 loss to Baltimore in Week 9 of the 2024 season. The fourth-quarter magic painted across so many of Denver’s victories last year never even threatened to show up at Arrowhead Stadium.
“I just felt like it was penalty after penalty after penalty,” said Nix, who fumbled as many times Monday (three) as he did during his entire rookie season in 2024. “Nobody has good plays to call when you’re in second-and-long and third-and-long. I mean, the play sheet is very small. We just didn’t put anybody in a good spot today. We really didn’t.”
The most curious aspect of Webb’s first night in the play-calling seat was Denver’s pass-run imbalance when the game was still to be decided. The Broncos were either tied or trailing by one touchdown throughout the first half. Yet, when the second quarter ended, the Broncos had dropped back to pass 19 times and handed the ball to their running backs only five times, including only three carries for starter J.K. Dobbins. It wasn’t until Kenneth Walker’s 60-yard run gave Kansas City a 21-7 lead early in the third quarter — on a fourth-and-1 play, no less — that the Broncos started consistently trying to run the football. Payton noted that some of the pass attempts were the result of Nix choosing to keep the ball on calls that had run-pass options, but the bottom line was that Denver couldn’t match the Chiefs’ physical tone on the ground.
“They rushed the ball well and we didn’t,” Payton said. “That starts with me. That starts with our coaching staff. … Regardless of who is calling the plays, if you’re the head coach, it’s frustrating; it’s disappointing. I don’t know that the feeling is any different, whether you’re calling them or not.”
Nobody on the offensive side of the ball for the Broncos sounded alarms after the game. They have too much experience and too many proven playmakers to believe games like the opener will be the norm. And they have too much confidence in Webb to believe a rocky night against the Chiefs and maestro defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo was indicative of who he will be in that role going forward.
Nix said Webb will respond to Monday’s letdown “exactly like he would have responded with a win.”
“He would have said it wasn’t good enough and that we’ve got to find ways to get back and continue (to improve) the next week,” the quarterback added. “He’s going to move on really well.”
Webb took over for a coach in Payton who would at times last season write “Run The Ball!” on his play sheet as a big-picture reminder of how the Broncos needed to play. His review of Monday’s game will reveal opportunities that were missed early against the Chiefs. Another note that needs to be jotted down in the debrief: Denver can’t have another game in which Waddle and Courtland Sutton combine for only three catches and 13 yards.
The explosive plays and points need to be found quickly. The Broncos next host a Jaguars team that gave up only 10 points in its Week 1 opener against the Browns and gave Denver’s offense fits when the two teams met last December. There is no let up after that, with games against the Rams, 49ers, Chargers and Seahawks rounding out a grueling six-game start to the season.
There is no panic. There is also little time to lose in what Payton calls “the race to improve” early in the season.
“The culture that’s been building here for four years, we come back from this stuff,” tight end Adam Trautman said. “We always have and that’s what I expect out of us.”

full_text:
Kenneth Walker III stood out in his Chiefs debut with 173 yards and a score in Monday night's win over the Broncos. David Eulitt / Getty Images
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — Kingsley Suamataia sat in front of his locker, his voice soft even if his words spoke volumes.
In the aftermath of a dominating Kansas City Chiefs win — a 31-10 Week 1 trouncing of the Denver Broncos — the left guard was asked what his team’s offense had shown the NFL world during its “Monday Night Football” showcase.
“That’s Chiefs football: point blank, period,” Suamataia said. “That’s how Chiefs football is played: It’s bullyball, smashmouth ball, and let’s get it going.”
It’s worth appreciating now: Those sentences would’ve made no sense to the outside world some four hours earlier.
These Chiefs, paced by former MVP quarterback Patrick Mahomes, a bullyball team? This team, led by a coach in Andy Reid who loves throwing it around the yard, winning with smashmouth ball ?
It was the biggest storyline of a night when the Chiefs ran for 220 yards and won by three scores while Mahomes — by his own admission — was pedestrian at best.
So what all played into it? An aggressive mindset up front. A greater emphasis on physicality and finishing under new offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy.
And most of all, a transcendent addition in free-agent running back Kenneth Walker III, who was dazzling in his Chiefs debut, rushing 23 times for a career-high 173 yards.
“It’s just a special ability to run the ball tough, between the tackles,” Mahomes said, “and then when he does bounce it, he has the speed to go all the way.”
Walker showed that — spectacularly — early in the third quarter.
The Chiefs faced a fourth-and-1 at their own 40. They went to a jumbo package with extra linemen that had worked earlier, believing they could outmuscle the Broncos to pick up a tough yard.
Except, it didn’t really work out that way. Denver’s defensive line got penetration and knocked off pulling guard Trey Smith. Chiefs defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga — subbed in as a fullback — didn’t deliver the hoped-for block on the edge.
Rookie running back Emmett Johnson said afterward that this type of scenario can be when a running back panics. When everything gets clogged up, the tendency can be to put your head down and try to make a hole when none is there.
Facing this situation, though, the veteran Walker didn’t flinch. He saw Broncos cornerback Riley Moss come too far inside, staying patient in a moment of chaos.
“I knew they were going to crash in,” Walker said. “When they crashed in, I bounced it out.”
Walker stepped through Moss’ tackle attempt, then sprinted down the sideline on his way to a 60-yard touchdown dash.
All on a play that wasn’t otherwise executed as the Chiefs planned.
“That fourth down and 1 was a thing of beauty,” Reid said.
“Once he gets the edge,” Mahomes said, “he’s gone.”
“He’s a beast,” Tonga said. “I was just trying to find a block for him, and I didn’t really need to.”
It was like this all night as Walker embarrassed a Broncos defense that couldn’t bring him down — or really, anyone else.
NFL Next Gen Stats data showed the Broncos missing 28 tackles while allowing 247 yards after those attempts. It was the highest yardage total allowed by a defense since at least 2018.
And all that just gave the Chiefs more confidence to continue a run-first game plan. K.C., in fact, went with designed runs on 50.8 percent of its plays Monday, per TruMedia, marking just the second time since 2022 that the Chiefs’ runs outnumbered their passes.
The belief in that vision trickled through the team.
It included the receivers room, as wideouts like Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton flashed with run blocking in their first game playing for Bieniemy and new receivers coach Chad O’Shea.
Rice, speaking to reporters afterward, also revealed a catchphrase that helped shape his mindset: “If you don’t block, you don’t get the rock.”
“We did great in the running game. There’s a lot of plays where I’m getting in there, motioning down to that line, gotta put my head down and block a linebacker probably 15 times a day,” Rice said. “We’re all just doing our job. It don’t really matter.”
The toughest part of keeping up with that physicality? On Monday, Rice acknowledged that he tried to focus on his assignment when he really wanted to turn around and see what Walker would do next.
The former Seattle Seahawks running back was that good. Walker had two 20-plus-yard runs — Chiefs running backs combined for one all of last season — and also contributed to the pass game while tying for the team lead with three receptions.
His presence also gave K.C. faith to go with the ground-first focus as they eased some guys into action. That included Mahomes, who played in his first game since tearing the ACL and LCL in his left knee nine months ago, and also undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson, who started at left tackle after not taking one snap at that position during his college career.
Benson became the first undrafted rookie to start Week 1 for Reid in his 14 seasons with the Chiefs.
Walker didn’t just get praise from offensive players. As he was leaving his postgame news conference, he came face to face with defensive tackle Chris Jones, who spoke loud enough so a roomful of reporters could hear him.
“That’s my hero,” Jones said with a smile.
The unanswered question now: What comes next?
Coming off a disappointing 6-11 season, Monday night’s game mattered for the Chiefs as they try to re-establish their dynasty-type ways after appearances in the three previous Super Bowls. Through that stretch, though, they mostly relied on Mahomes’ brilliance and clutch play, as he tended to elevate his game in the most important moments.
Monday, then, was something different. Mahomes completed only 15 of 27 passes for 184 yards. He threw a bad interception on a miscommunication with receiver Xavier Worthy.
In the past, the Chiefs likely would have chalked those performances up as immediate losses. So what happens if they happen in three-possession wins?
“We talked about it all week long: Against this defense, you’ve got to set the tone,” Mahomes said in his “Monday Night Football” postgame interview. “That offensive line and those running backs did that.”
Rice said this was certainly a different feeling. With the game in control late, he said he turned to one of his teammates on the sideline and said, “This is probably how the Chiefs used to be before I got here.”
Those glory days — the ones when Mahomes was putting up video-game statistics — were part of an era when the offense felt inevitable.
“So I guess we’re getting back to our original self,” Rice said with a grin. “We’re just gonna keep growing.”
The next test will tell us something. Indianapolis comes to Arrowhead Stadium on Sunday and will arrive fully knowing the first version of the Chiefs’ 2026 offense didn’t quite look like past editions.
These Chiefs? For a night? They won with their mindset — and also their physicality.
“To come out the first game like that and just punch them in the mouth as a team,” Suamataia said, “it was really fun.”

Every week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.

full_text:
Devin Singletary and the Giants surprised the favored Cowboys behind a strong all-around performance on Sunday night. Elsa / Getty Images
Every week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
Week 1 was a doozy! The best team in the league — a “superteam,” or so we thought based on our initial power rankings — got hammered, a Super Bowl rematch didn’t change the result from February, at least three Super Bowl contenders opened with a loss and points were way up .
With that, the first week of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, and we finally have some meaningful results to examine. So let’s take a look in this week’s power rankings at what we learned from each team.
What we learned: The offense is still humming
After the franchise’s drama-filled offseason and with questions about the aging roster, the 49ers had no trouble moving the ball against the Rams. Brock Purdy threw for three touchdowns, the running game (including rookie Kaelon Black) looked good and Raheem Morris’ defense was great. It’d be hard to draw up a better start.
Up next: vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Beat Patriots 13-10
What we learned: That run defense is still elite
Against a Patriots team that spent its whole offseason focused on running the ball better after getting humiliated in the Super Bowl, the Seahawks’ run defense dominated once again. Seattle limited New England to 2.5 yards per attempt on its designed rushes. Plenty is still unknown about how long Sam Darnold will be out, but — no surprise — the defense is still great.
Up next: at Cardinals, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
What we learned: They’re the AFC favorites
The Bills were a trendy pick to reach the Super Bowl this season, even in their first year under new coach Joe Brady. They showed why on Sunday. The Texans might have the best defense in the NFL, yet the Bills put up 409 yards of offense while Josh Allen threw for a pair of touchdowns and added another two on the ground. That offense will be fun for the home crowd to watch as Buffalo unveils its new stadium Thursday night.
Up next: vs. Lions, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
1-0. pic.twitter.com/XguSOY6RL8
— Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 13, 2026
Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37
What we learned: Best offense in the NFL?
Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
What we learned: The young OC might work
The Ravens raised some eyebrows around the league during the offseason when they hired a 29-year-old offensive coordinator. Declan Doyle is now 30, but the young coach and a healthy Lamar Jackson led to an impressive rout in Week 1 that featured 506 yards of offense.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Thursday: Lost to 49ers 27-7
What we learned: Sleep helps
The season didn’t start well for the NFL’s superteam that has Super Bowl-or-bust aspirations. Matthew Stafford, the defending league MVP, threw for just 155 yards with no touchdowns and an interception in Australia. Now Myles Garrett is on injured reserve and out for at least four games.
Up next: vs. Giants, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Monday: Beat Broncos 31-10
What we learned: They have a running game!
After dealing with an inconsistent ground attack last season, the Chiefs went out and signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III. It took Walker one game to make a big impact. All eyes in the opener were on Patrick Mahomes’ return, but it was Walker who stole the show, totaling 191 yards of offense and two touchdowns, and adding a new dimension to the K.C. offense.
Up next: vs. Colts, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Saints 31-30 (OT)
What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble
The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown.
Up next: at Bills, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Bills 36-31
What we learned: The defense is beatable
That side of the ball is supposed to carry this team. Even though the Bills had the ball for under 24 minutes of game time, the Texans’ usually dominant defense still got gashed at home. C.J. Stroud was better Sunday than in the playoffs, which is the last time we saw him, but his strip-sack in the final seconds cemented Houston’s loss.
Up next: vs. Bengals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Lost to Seahawks 13-10
What we learned: Drake Maye’s slump isn’t over
The Patriots had hoped that Maye’s four-game postseason slide last season was largely the result of a shoulder injury and some big games in bad weather against great defenses. But with a full offseason to prepare, Maye struggled again against the Seahawks, throwing three interceptions, including a brutal one in the end zone when New England easily could’ve forced overtime.
Up next: vs. Steelers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Commanders 24-22
What we learned: Jalen Hurts can still produce moments
The final box score isn’t going to instill a ton of faith that the Eagles’ offense has suddenly morphed back into one of the league’s best. But Hurts made enough big plays when his team needed him, connecting on a deep ball and improvising with his legs on a third-and-18 conversion to offer hope as Philadelphia settles into this new offensive scheme under Sean Mannion.
Up next: at Titans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Monday: Lost to Chiefs 31-10
What we learned: There’s concern on offense
In a bit of a surprise this offseason, coach Sean Payton relinquished offensive play-calling duties to 31-year-old coordinator Davis Webb. His debut didn’t go well. After a pair of offseason ankle surgeries, Bo Nix fumbled three times, threw an interception and managed just 4.7 yards per attempt, while new receiver Jaylen Waddle had only one catch for 2 yards.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Did we really learn anything about the Jaguars by watching them beat a hapless Browns team? Still, props to them for jumping out to a 31-0 lead and putting it on cruise control behind a great game from Trevor Lawrence and an impressive showing from the defense. Now, the schedule turns brutal with five straight games against teams with Super Bowl hopes.
Up next: at Broncos, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Buccaneers 33-27
What we learned: They have a defense!
The bar might have been on the floor for that side of the ball after last season, but the new-look Cincinnati defense came to play against Tampa Bay, forcing four turnovers and notching four sacks. It was an especially impressive win considering Ja’Marr Chase caught only two passes for 12 yards.
Up next: at Texans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 39-22
What we learned: Brian Flores is a mad man
And we mean that in a good way. The Minnesota defensive coordinator sent blitzes on 74 percent(!) of the Packers’ dropbacks and totally overwhelmed their offensive line late as the Vikings put together an impressive comeback win with backup quarterback Carson Wentz leading the offense.
Up next: at Bears, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 20-13
What we learned: Things look familiar
Yes, the Steelers have a new coach, but this team looked much like it has in recent years. The defense was pretty good. The offense was mostly fine. It’s rarely worth putting too much stock into Week 1, but this Mike McCarthy-led squad looks like another roughly .500 team. We should learn more about the Steelers in Week 2 during their trip to New England.
Up next: at Patriots, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 39-22
What we learned: New season, same Packers
That was the headline…
