Devin Singletary and the Giants surprised the favored Cowboys behind a strong all-around performance on Sunday night. Elsa / Getty Images
Every week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
Week 1 was a doozy! The best team in the league — a “superteam,” or so we thought based on our initial power rankings — got hammered, a Super Bowl rematch didn’t change the result from February, at least three Super Bowl contenders opened with a loss and points were way up .
With that, the first week of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, and we finally have some meaningful results to examine. So let’s take a look in this week’s power rankings at what we learned from each team.
What we learned: The offense is still humming
After the franchise’s drama-filled offseason and with questions about the aging roster, the 49ers had no trouble moving the ball against the Rams. Brock Purdy threw for three touchdowns, the running game (including rookie Kaelon Black) looked good and Raheem Morris’ defense was great. It’d be hard to draw up a better start.
Up next: vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Beat Patriots 13-10
What we learned: That run defense is still elite
Against a Patriots team that spent its whole offseason focused on running the ball better after getting humiliated in the Super Bowl, the Seahawks’ run defense dominated once again. Seattle limited New England to 2.5 yards per attempt on its designed rushes. Plenty is still unknown about how long Sam Darnold will be out, but — no surprise — the defense is still great.
Up next: at Cardinals, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
What we learned: They’re the AFC favorites
The Bills were a trendy pick to reach the Super Bowl this season, even in their first year under new coach Joe Brady. They showed why on Sunday. The Texans might have the best defense in the NFL, yet the Bills put up 409 yards of offense while Josh Allen threw for a pair of touchdowns and added another two on the ground. That offense will be fun for the home crowd to watch as Buffalo unveils its new stadium Thursday night.
Up next: vs. Lions, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
1-0. pic.twitter.com/XguSOY6RL8
— Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 13, 2026
Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37
What we learned: Best offense in the NFL?
Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
What we learned: The young OC might work
The Ravens raised some eyebrows around the league during the offseason when they hired a 29-year-old offensive coordinator. Declan Doyle is now 30, but the young coach and a healthy Lamar Jackson led to an impressive rout in Week 1 that featured 506 yards of offense.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Thursday: Lost to 49ers 27-7
What we learned: Sleep helps
The season didn’t start well for the NFL’s superteam that has Super Bowl-or-bust aspirations. Matthew Stafford, the defending league MVP, threw for just 155 yards with no touchdowns and an interception in Australia. Now Myles Garrett is on injured reserve and out for at least four games.
Up next: vs. Giants, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Monday: Beat Broncos 31-10
What we learned: They have a running game!
After dealing with an inconsistent ground attack last season, the Chiefs went out and signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III. It took Walker one game to make a big impact. All eyes in the opener were on Patrick Mahomes’ return, but it was Walker who stole the show, totaling 191 yards of offense and two touchdowns, and adding a new dimension to the K.C. offense.
Up next: vs. Colts, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Saints 31-30 (OT)
What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble
The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown.
Up next: at Bills, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Bills 36-31
What we learned: The defense is beatable
That side of the ball is supposed to carry this team. Even though the Bills had the ball for under 24 minutes of game time, the Texans’ usually dominant defense still got gashed at home. C.J. Stroud was better Sunday than in the playoffs, which is the last time we saw him, but his strip-sack in the final seconds cemented Houston’s loss.
Up next: vs. Bengals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Lost to Seahawks 13-10
What we learned: Drake Maye’s slump isn’t over
The Patriots had hoped that Maye’s four-game postseason slide last season was largely the result of a shoulder injury and some big games in bad weather against great defenses. But with a full offseason to prepare, Maye struggled again against the Seahawks, throwing three interceptions, including a brutal one in the end zone when New England easily could’ve forced overtime.
Up next: vs. Steelers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Commanders 24-22
What we learned: Jalen Hurts can still produce moments
The final box score isn’t going to instill a ton of faith that the Eagles’ offense has suddenly morphed back into one of the league’s best. But Hurts made enough big plays when his team needed him, connecting on a deep ball and improvising with his legs on a third-and-18 conversion to offer hope as Philadelphia settles into this new offensive scheme under Sean Mannion.
Up next: at Titans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Monday: Lost to Chiefs 31-10
What we learned: There’s concern on offense
In a bit of a surprise this offseason, coach Sean Payton relinquished offensive play-calling duties to 31-year-old coordinator Davis Webb. His debut didn’t go well. After a pair of offseason ankle surgeries, Bo Nix fumbled three times, threw an interception and managed just 4.7 yards per attempt, while new receiver Jaylen Waddle had only one catch for 2 yards.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Did we really learn anything about the Jaguars by watching them beat a hapless Browns team? Still, props to them for jumping out to a 31-0 lead and putting it on cruise control behind a great game from Trevor Lawrence and an impressive showing from the defense. Now, the schedule turns brutal with five straight games against teams with Super Bowl hopes.
Up next: at Broncos, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Buccaneers 33-27
What we learned: They have a defense!
The bar might have been on the floor for that side of the ball after last season, but the new-look Cincinnati defense came to play against Tampa Bay, forcing four turnovers and notching four sacks. It was an especially impressive win considering Ja’Marr Chase caught only two passes for 12 yards.
Up next: at Texans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 39-22
What we learned: Brian Flores is a mad man
And we mean that in a good way. The Minnesota defensive coordinator sent blitzes on 74 percent(!) of the Packers’ dropbacks and totally overwhelmed their offensive line late as the Vikings put together an impressive comeback win with backup quarterback Carson Wentz leading the offense.
Up next: at Bears, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 20-13
What we learned: Things look familiar
Yes, the Steelers have a new coach, but this team looked much like it has in recent years. The defense was pretty good. The offense was mostly fine. It’s rarely worth putting too much stock into Week 1, but this Mike McCarthy-led squad looks like another roughly .500 team. We should learn more about the Steelers in Week 2 during their trip to New England.
Up next: at Patriots, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 39-22
What we learned: New season, same Packers
That was the headline…

full_text:
Maxx Crosby managed 1.5 sacks Sunday despite playing fewer snaps than usual. David Brytus / Imagn Images
HENDERSON, Nev. — The Las Vegas Raiders had a plan to manage star edge rusher Maxx Crosby during their Week 1 win over the Miami Dolphins, head coach Klint Kubiak confirmed.
Crosby underwent knee surgery in January to repair a torn meniscus, ending his 2025 season. The injury caused the Baltimore Ravens to rescind their acquisition of him in March, failing him on his physical and sending him back to Las Vegas.
Crosby grew tired of discussing concerns about his knee throughout the offseason, saying he felt healthy and ready to go. He showed that upon returning to the field during training camp, dominating practices and looking like the five-time Pro Bowler he is. But Kubiak kept him out of the preseason, saving his first real game action since surgery until the season opener.
Crosby played 46 of the Raiders’ 56 defensive snaps against the Dolphins. It marked just the fourth time that Crosby’s snap share was 82 percent or lower since 2023. He’s been on the field for 94 percent or more of the Raiders’ defensive plays in each of the past four seasons.
It was difficult to determine a pattern in Crosby’s useage. He played the first two defensive drives in full, during which Las Vegas forced two punts. Crosby then sat out the first six plays of the third defensive drive, when Miami gained 34 yards and got into Raiders’ territory. Crosby then came in and immediately stopped a run behind the line of scrimmage, helping Las Vegas hold Miami to a field goal.
When asked why Crosby was out for the start of the drive, Kubiak said postgame: “That’s just my call.”
Crosby played the entirety of the Dolphins’ last drive of the first half (Miami kicked a field goal) and the opening drive of the second half (quarterback Malik Willis scrambled for a touchdown to Crosby’s side). He then missed the first two snaps of Miami’s next drive, which ended with Willis throwing an interception to rookie safety Treydan Stukes. Crosby returned for the next drive, then missed the Dolphins’ first two offensive plays of the fourth quarter before playing the rest of the game.
Whatever the Raiders’ plan was for managing Crosby, it appeared to keep him fresh. He had a third-down sack of Willis on his first play of the fourth quarter to force a punt, and combined with Kwity Paye for another takedown of the quarterback on the next third down. Crosby totaled 1.5 sacks and 8 pressures, his most in a game since Week 13 of the 2024 season, according to TruMedia.
“It was amazing, I’ve been waiting a long time,” Crosby said of how he felt postgame. “It’s been a long rehab, long offseason, a lot of things that I had to go through, a lot of hurdles and things that I don’t think the everyday person gets to really see and the true grind of that. But I got to credit all the people around me that helped me get back out on that field. Had the best time. It’s just back playing football, doing what I love the most, and we definitely could do better. But off to a good start.”
It’s unclear what the Raiders’ plan with Crosby will be going forward. They don’t want to keep him off the field much; their defensive front suffered when he was on the sidelines. But in his eighth season coming off the knee surgery, they’ll want to do everything they can to keep him this effective.
Kubiak described star tight end Brock Bowers as “day-to-day.” The star tight end missed the win over the Dolphins after undergoing a surgery to “clean up” an issue with his knee .
Kubiak said Friday that he was initially optimistic Bowers would be able to play in Week 1, even after the surgery. Bowers was then seen after Sunday’s game walking, unaided, out of the locker room with a sleeve on his left leg. Kubiak said Monday that Bowers is “working his tail off to get back out on the field” and said it is “really important to him to play as soon as possible.”
Bowers suffered a knee injury in Week 1 last season that lingered throughout the year, ultimately causing a decline in his production and landing him on season-ending injured reserve in late December. When asked about the importance of not rushing Bowers back this year, Kubiak said he will listen to wellness coordinator Alex Guerrero and the team’s training staff.
“We’re gonna be smart with him, but if he’s ready to play, he’s gonna play,” Kubiak said.
The Raiders totaled 290 yards of offense against the Dolphins without their top receiving threat — 160 of which came through the air. Tight end Michael Mayer was the top target, catching six of the seven passes thrown his way for 32 yards. Wideout Tre Tucker led the Raiders with 42 receiving yards.
When asked whether the offense should derive confidence from a solid performance without Bowers, Kubiak said they should. But the team certainly wants him back as soon as possible.
Starting corner Darien Porter is also considered “day-to-day” with a foot injury, according to Kubiak. He went down trying to make a tackle during the fourth quarter against the Dolphins and did not return. He wore a walking boot in the locker room postgame.
In Porter’s absence, fifth-round rookie Hezekiah Masses stepped in. He broke up a pass on his first NFL defensive snap.
Quarterback Kirk Cousins led the Raiders to victory in his first start for the team. Kubiak said the 15-year veteran played “winning football,” but also had things “we’re going to get fixed and cleaned up.” Much of those issues arose downfield.
Cousins was dialed in on his short throws. He went 20-for-23 on passes 10 yards or less, for 139 yards and all 3 of his touchdowns. His 131.4 passer rating was second-best on such throws in Week 1, behind New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart. Cousins looked decisive as he worked through his reads, and he was on-target for some intermediate throws that turned into big plays, such as when he threaded his touchdown to receiver Jack Bech.
But when he tried to throw beyond 10 yards, things weren’t so clean. He was 1-for-7 on such attempts, with his only completion coming on play-action, when Tucker was wide open for a 21-yard gain. Cousins’ two interceptions came on throws of 13 and 20 air yards, and his 0 passer rating on attempts over 10 yards was the league’s worst in Week 1.
Kubiak said Cousins’ interceptions were “avoidable mistakes” that the quarterback will want back. He overthrew Bech on a crossing route, allowing Dolphins rookie safety Michael Taaffe to easily pick off the first one. And he second-guessed targeting a wide-open Jalen Nailor over the middle on his second pick, his indecision allowing safety Dante Trader Jr. to intercept. Kubiak said they’ll learn from the mistakes, but thought that Cousins opened the game “playing really good football.”
When asked what needs to happen to get more going downfield in the passing game, Kubiak said Miami did a good job of limiting explosives. Bowers’ eventual return will make it harder for opposing teams to do so, but Cousins appears limited in making deep throws at this point in his career. They’ll need him to improve on such passes going forward — Kubiak said it’s important to develop a vertical threat to open up the offense.
Even while still recovering from an ankle injury, running back Ashton Jeanty dominated the backfield share against the Dolphins, playing 50 offensive snaps (74%). Rookie Mike Washington Jr., who was in line to start if Jeanty couldn’t go, got 13 snaps (19%) in his NFL debut.
Jeanty earned the right to stay on the field as he totaled 147 yards from scrimmage and caught two touchdowns. Washington also looked good in his limited opportunities, rushing for 41 yards and 5.9 per carry. But Kubiak said he wanted to give Jeanty all the chances he could with how he was playing.
“Most games I’ve been in, it never turns out exactly how you plan it,” Kubiak said. “A lot of times, you’re riding the guy that has the hot hand. We’ve got two guys who are playing good football. Ashton,…

title: Vikings' Kevin O'Connell opting for substance over stats: 'It's about winning' O’Connell has no problem with winning ugly: “You learn it doesn’t matter what the stat box looks like.” Alec Lewis 33

full_text:
Kevin O'Connell of the Vikings was the NFL's Coach of the Year in 2024. But his team's offensive struggles last season forced him to reevaluate his priorities. Adam Bettcher / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Reach the inner circle, and you earn an opportunity to establish a name. Sean McVay has. Mike Macdonald is starting to.
First, they became NFL head coaches. Then, their success on offense or defense became something of a brand. Pundits praise their systems and play calls. Players rave about their knowledge, explanations and adaptability.
The media ecosystem, which often rewards glitz and glamor, almost adds incentive to pursue that guru status.
On Sunday evening, following his team’s impressive comeback victory over the Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell came close to admitting this. His team had won a massive season opener in semi-ugly fashion. In the aftermath, O’Connell explained how experience helped him realize that the most elite coaches in the inner circle care not about the appearance but about the final result.
“I don’t think, in some of the adversity (the Vikings have faced in recent years), I’ve coached very well,” O’Connell said. “Trying to maybe worry about the stat sheet (hurt the team). Trying to maybe worry about what it’s going to look like when you pick up the newspaper. Statistically, are people going to think you’re a good coach?
That this came pouring out in response to an otherwise mundane question about quarterback Carson Wentz speaks to its revelatory nature.
It also doesn’t hurt that O’Connell backed those words with action.
After months of discussion about revamping the team’s run game, O’Connell stuck with the ground game against the Packers, even despite early struggles.
In fact, the Vikings ran the ball 27 times when trailing Sunday. That’s the second-highest total since O’Connell became the Vikings’ head coach in 2022. In 2024, in a sloppy matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars, Minnesota ran the ball 28 times to ease pressure on then-quarterback Sam Darnold.
The renewed commitment to the run game — especially amid suboptimal quarterback circumstances — represents a deeper attentiveness to the complementary nature required for that specific week.
Unprompted, Vikings right tackle Brian O’Neill brought up O’Connell’s run-game commitment after the game. The Vikings only averaged 3.6 yards per carry, with a subpar 32.1 percent success rate. Critically, though, running back Jordan Mason broke free for a 28-yard outside-zone hit on the team’s go-ahead drive . Both he and Aaron Jones scored on short touchdown runs.
“We weren’t really hitting any big ones,” O’Neill said, “but we just kept calling them and calling them and calling them. And, like, that’s pretty cool. Eventually, they’re going to pop. And they did.”
O’Connell arrived in Minnesota with considerable offensive acclaim. He had helped reorient the Los Angeles Rams’ offense around the strengths of Matthew Stafford. His work played a major role in the Rams’ Super Bowl LVI title.
Speak with his former players and colleagues, and they will laud O’Connell’s innate ability to identify coverages in real time and formulate a concise plan of attack amid the noise of competition.
With this backdrop came high expectations. He would design an offense around superstar receiver Justin Jefferson. He would create a beneficial environment, centered on positivity, around veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins. And O’Connell validated many of those beliefs. That, paired with his real-time piloting of Josh Dobbs’ extraordinary Vikings debut in 2023, earned him a particular reputation.
Darnold’s bounce-back 2024 season provided punctuation. The Vikings won 14 regular-season games, and O’Connell was named the NFL Coach of the Year.
Maintaining the prestige of an offensive mastermind means building atop what has already been accomplished. That becomes harder when the quarterback position shifts from a trustworthy veteran to a raw second-year player.
O’Connell entered the 2025 season intending to streamline the task for J.J. McCarthy. That attempt, and McCarthy’s own issues with accuracy and reliability, didn’t jibe with the desire to target Jefferson and light up the scoreboard.
Eventually, O’Connell altered the recipe to a simpler blend. The Vikings utilized heavy personnel on early downs to stay efficient, and they schemed third-down concepts angled toward the sidelines. Those choices won.
“You learn it doesn’t matter what the stat box looks like,” O’Connell said in the lead-up to Sunday’s game. “It doesn’t matter what the EPA (expected points added) looks like. You need to know those things to know how teams may view what you’re successful at. But none of those things matter. Winning is the only thing that matters.”
The offseason signing of Kyler Murray gave the Vikings and O’Connell a chance to revert to their flashier plans. But they haven’t really gotten the opportunity.
Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon darted into the backfield to torpedo a run play on the first snap. Later, linebacker Edgerrin Cooper flew around linemen and snatched Vikings running backs on two separate snaps. Minnesota’s offense trudged forward with conviction.
Rather than placing all of the responsibility on Wentz’s shoulders, the Vikings incorporated 21 or 22 personnel on almost 40 percent of their offensive snaps, the highest percentage of any game in O’Connell’s tenure. The heavy-package runs worked like jabs in a boxing ring. The Vikings chipped away at the Packers long enough to spring Mason at a critical juncture in the game.
With that said, perhaps the most underrated benefit of this strategy could surface next week.
Trot out onto the field with big bodies, and the Chicago Bears will have good reason to expect a rush around the edge. Start messing with opponents’ expectations effectively, and the Vikings can create mismatches on the field. Find success, and an NFL coach just might force his way into the elite tier of the coaching inner circle.

full_text:
New York Giants QB Jaxson Dart on coach John Harbaugh: "The identity of the team starts at the top, and it starts with how he's conducted himself, with how he's created a tough team.” Vincent Carchietta / Imagn Images
There were days during the New York Giants’ grueling training camp this summer that even left tackle Andrew Thomas, who has impeccable football character, was worn down. But the Giants not only survived their first training camp with coach John Harbaugh, they saw the fruits of their laborious practices in their 28-20 win over the Cowboys in Sunday’s season opener.
“We were definitely conditioned for the fourth quarter,” Thomas said. “We practice hard. Sometimes I’m not too happy at practice, but it definitely pays off.”
Harbaugh’s resume gave him instant credibility throughout the organization and in the locker room. But the buy-in could fade if the results don’t follow the hard work. That’s why Sunday’s impressive start has made the Giants even stronger believers in Harbaugh’s methods.
“I don’t think anyone would shy away from saying it was the hardest training camp of their career,” 10th-year veteran right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “I’ve been around Harbs (in Baltimore), and this was a physical-ass training camp. Now you know why you run that many plays in practice, why you hit as much, why you do those practices, why you lift as much as we do, how hard we work because you go out there on Sunday and, you really beat a team up like that.”
There was a different feel to Sunday’s home prime-time matchup with a rival that had dominated the series for a decade. MetLife Stadium was electric, full of fans starving for success and buoyed by the arrival of Harbaugh.
“Seeing the crowd out there tonight, they had a huge impact in the game, just the energy and momentum,” quarterback Jaxson Dart said. “That stuff’s huge. So just everybody showing up, showing out on a big night like tonight, where it was bigger than even just the game itself, was just a really special environment to be in.”
The most encouraging aspect of Sunday’s win was how much the performance fit the vision Harbaugh has outlined since his arrival. The Giants were the more physical team from start to finish.
“We have so much respect for Coach Harbs, and this team will do whatever he says, because we have all the faith in him that he’s going to put us in the best situation to win,” Dart said. “The identity of the team starts at the top, and it starts with how he’s conducted himself, with how he’s created a tough team.”
Here are four more takeaways from the Giants’ first home win in Week 1 since 2010:
The Giants scored 28 points while producing just one play from scrimmage that gained more than 20 yards: a 22-yard run by Dart that had an additional 15 yards tacked on for an unnecessary roughness penalty on Dallas. The Giants ground through multiple lengthy possessions, with four of their seven drives lasting at least 10 plays. That was the formula to neutralize an explosive Cowboys offense. It will likely be the blueprint again in Week 2 against a Rams offense that is expected to be high-octane despite a sluggish performance in a 27-7 loss to the 49ers in their season opener.
“I don’t know if methodical would be our identity throughout the entire season,” Dart said. “I think that was just what was needed to win this game.”
The Giants enjoyed an overwhelming 21:33 to 8:27 advantage in time of possession in the second half. The Cowboys scored touchdowns on both of their second-half possessions, but the Giants didn’t give them enough opportunities to mount a comeback.
Being efficient is paramount with such a methodical approach. The Giants scored touchdowns on all four of their red-zone trips. They were 9-for-10 on third downs (excluding a kneeldown on the final third down of the game). The Giants converted all four of their third-and-longs. That rate isn’t sustainable, which is why Dart is counting on producing more explosives. But it was impressive to see Dart consistently deliver when facing unfavorable circumstances.
It’s no surprise that the Giants converted both times they had third-and-1 because they drilled short-yardage endlessly during training camp. The Giants ran a modified version of the tush push, with 300-pound fullback Pat Ricard motioning behind Dart to help the quarterback surge forward on his sneaks.
Ricard’s value can’t be measured in the box score. The fumble recovery he had after tight end Isaiah Likely was stripped on the last play of the first quarter may be Ricard’s only touch of the season. But Ricard is vital to the rushing attack, as he played 54 percent of the offensive snaps and was frequently sent in pre-snap motion as a lead blocker.
Ricard has been a favorite of Harbaugh’s since he was converted from defensive tackle to fullback as an undrafted rookie out of Maine in 2017.
“Nobody in the world can do some of the things that Pat Ricard can do,” Harbaugh said. “And that’s good for us. That’s unique for us.”
Ricard’s fumble recovery, which was especially important in a game with limited possessions, demonstrated his awareness. But when an oblong ball hits the turf, there’s often an equal chance the other team will recover, so Harbaugh was predictably unhappy with his team’s four fumbles against Dallas.
Caleb Downs with a HUGE hit on Jaxson Dart 😤
DALvsNYG on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/6x4h1EbLxb
— NFL (@NFL) September 14, 2026
Dart never saw unblocked blitzer Caleb Downs, who hit the quarterback and jarred the ball loose into the arms of Giants left guard Jon Runyan in the second quarter. Running back Cam Skattebo lost the ball on a fourth-quarter run, but was fortunate that it bounced right back to him.
Running back Tyrone Tracy’s fumble in the second quarter was no different than the others, except that it was recovered by Dallas to kill a promising drive. It continued a miserable stretch for Tracy, who also had a fumble in the preseason. With his spot on the depth chart already hanging by a thread, Tracy didn’t play another offensive snap after.
The Giants made veteran running back Najee Harris, who signed late in the preseason as he returns from a torn Achilles, a healthy scratch for the opener. Tracy’s fumble could be his final strike, with him swapping spots with Harris and being inactive in Week 2.
“One of those non-negotiables is ball security. We’re putting the ball on the ground entirely too much,” Harbaugh said. “We’ve got to make sure (we’re) better, because the ball’s on the ground four times, and that’s just not even close to being acceptable.”
Reliable veteran Devin Singletary already had taken Tracy’s role as the third-down back. Singletary strengthened his hold on that job with four catches for 22 yards and a touchdown.
The Giants mixed their offensive personnel at a dizzying pace. Rookie Malachi Fields led the wide receivers by playing 72 percent of the offensive snaps. Fields made two catches for 25 yards and was twice targeted on deep shots that just missed connecting. Fields’ blocking ability will assure him of playing time in the Giants’ power rushing offense.
Malik Nabers played 52 percent of the snaps on a pitch count in his first game back from a knee injury. He fielded a team-high nine targets on just 24 pass plays, finishing with six catches for 69 yards. That’s a sign of how much Nabers will be the focal point of the passing attack when he’s fully back.
Darnell Mooney recorded two catches for 27 yards while playing 57 percent of the snaps. Surprisingly, Braxton Berrios played 17 percent of the snaps. He wasn’t targeted, but was deployed creatively. He lined up in the backfield on three snaps and was often used in motion as eye candy for the defense, most notably on a fake jet sweep that helped Likely get open for a 2-yard touchdown catch. It appears Berrios is being used for some of the plays that had been planned for Calvin Austin, who tore his ACL late in training camp.

title: Why Malik Nabers' mom wasn't at Giants game for WR's return: 'He had to do this by himself' Charlotte Carroll 10
summary:

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Since Malik Nabers’ days at LSU suiting up for the Tigers, his mom, Tonya Nabers, hasn’t missed a game.
Through the wide receiver’s three seasons in Baton Rouge, La., to a record-setting rookie campaign after being drafted No. 6 overall by the New York Giants to a sophomore season cut short by a devastating injury, Tonya has been there for it all, watching h
full_text:
Malik Nabers caught six passes for 69 yards in his return to the Giants on Sunday night. Brad Penner / Imagn Images
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Since Malik Nabers’ days at LSU suiting up for the Tigers, his mom, Tonya Nabers, hasn’t missed a game.
Through the wide receiver’s three seasons in Baton Rouge, La., to a record-setting rookie campaign after being drafted No. 6 overall by the New York Giants to a sophomore season cut short by a devastating injury, Tonya has been there for it all, watching her son become a superstar in front of the football-watching world.
But on Sunday night at MetLife Stadium, as Nabers helped the Giants upset the Dallas Cowboys 28-20 in front of a frenzied Week 1 crowd, she wasn’t among the Big Blue faithful.
“This game, Malik had to do this by himself,” Tonya told The Athletic on Monday. “He needed to go out there with no pressure from anybody and just perform.”
Instead of watching her son from the stands, she watched her son on TV with her sister in Houston.
“It worked out perfectly because if I had been there, I wouldn’t have been able to hide my emotion or my fear,” she said. “He would have been able to sense that I was nervous or my anxiety was high, and I think I would have made him uneasy. So God’s timing is the best timing. And so this journey he needed to take by himself.”
Nabers may have spent the days and weeks leading up to Week 1 wrestling with whether he felt ready, both physically and mentally, to return from a torn ACL and meniscus, but for so long, Nabers hasn’t been by himself.
In the stands last Sept. 28, for the Giants’ Week 4 game against the Los Angeles Chargers, Tonya first thought Nabers suffered a shoulder injury after he landed hard on the MetLife Stadium field turf. It wasn’t until the cart came out that she realized something more serious had happened. When she saw Nabers being carried away from the field, Tonya left her seat, determined to find her son as he grappled with the agony of the first major injury of his career.
For months after the injury, Tonya helped her son navigate life post-surgery. She helped him get to physical therapy; she cooked some of his favorite foods — red beans and rice, fried chicken, cornbread and smothered cabbage — and she tried to help him negotiate the ups-and-downs of the rehab. From watching Nabers first trust his knee enough to put weight on it, to being able to walk down the stairs like he did pre-injury, Tonya was there for every milestone — big and small — on Nabers’ road to recovery.
Still, there were times during the process, Nabers admitted this summer, that he thought he’d never run a route again. That road to recovery isn’t without obstacles.
As Nabers wrestled with hurdles that stood in his way, the noise of a 24/7 NFL news cycle desperate to know Nabers’ next steps swirled around them. With Nabers not starting training camp on the physically unable to perform list, optimism grew that he could be ready for Week 1.
“I’ve heard a lot of people say it takes a little while for you to feel better, but I’ve put in countless hours of work; I’ve put in many nights,” Nabers said in late August. “I’ve sat in rooms, cried. I did everything to get to this moment, right here. So, I feel like when I get out there, I feel like I’ll be better than what I was before. I’ve put in the work. I went through everything that I could just to get to this moment.”
A week before the game, Nabers told his mom he wasn’t sure if he’d play. All she cared about was that he could play without any doubts.
In the final days leading into the opener, coach John Harbaugh deemed Nabers “ready to go,” but said it would be up to Nabers to make the final decision about whether he’d step onto the field Sunday against Dallas.
While he was a full participant in practice all week, Nabers was officially designated as questionable for the game, setting up a suspenseful 48 hours ahead of the Giants’ prime-time matchup against a bitter rival.
If you think it was only fans and the media that didn’t know Nabers’ status for Sunday, you’d be wrong. It was the Giants coaches, the front office, his family. Everyone was in the dark on the decision. Nabers’ teammates were hopeful during pregame warmups, but they didn’t want to ask; even quarterback Jaxson Dart said he kept his distance while he hoped for the best.
“I really didn’t know,” Nabers later said. “My family didn’t even come to this game because it’s a one-on-one battle that you have to go through. You have to do it for yourself. I didn’t want everybody here. I didn’t want my family here, and I feel like I (would have) let them down by not playing, so I had to do it for myself first.”
While Nabers said he made his decision after warmups, Tonya thinks he made the call even sooner than that — even if he didn’t know it.
“When I saw him walk through the stadium to go through the locker room and the way he was dressed with that smile, I know my son,” Tonya said. “I knew at that point he was gonna play.”
Malik Nabers is in the building #giants pic.twitter.com/DTfJSQAV16
— Charlotte Carroll (@charlottecrrll) September 13, 2026
Even a moment when she saw him take the field for pregame warmups in a hooded sweatshirt wasn’t enough to change her mind as she headed to her sister Faydra Nabers-Allen’s house in Houston to watch the game.
“One thing I know about her motherhood is that she’s always been so respectful of Malik and his career and his decision-making,” Nabers-Allen told The Athletic. “As sisters, we kind of looked at each other eye to eye, and we knew that whatever decision was on the table, it was a decision between Malik and God. … And when we saw him out there with his jersey on, we knew he had been very grounded in his decision, and so we did what we always do, and that’s cheer him on from right where we were.”
As the clock ticked down to kickoff and the team continued warmups, Nabers walked around the field a bit, at one point stepping into the end zone to raise his arms and pump up fans. He shared moments with teammates who approached him, including Dart.
Nabers was taking it all back in.
“You only get so long to play this game,” Nabers said afterward. “I feel like you know you got to take in every game. You never know when it’s gonna be your last. You never know when it’s gonna come away from you. You never know when it’s gonna be taken away. So, just taking in every moment and just still having fun while playing.”
Nabers soaked it all in, from the roar of the crowd when his name was announced as he ran out of the tunnel, to hearing fans screaming “Leeeeek” every time he caught the ball, which happened to be six times for 69 yards on a team-high nine targets. Nabers looked increasingly like his old self as the game went on, like he trusted his body to do what he needed it to.
That’s probably why Nabers seemed to have a smile on his face most of the night, though the one at the end of the game came after Dart handed him the game ball.
DART MADE SURE NABERS GOT THE GAME BALL 🥺
Malik Nabers was a game-time decision before the Giants’ win and hadn't played since September 2025 ❤️
(📺 NBC) pic.twitter.com/u0rn9hzNiP
— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) September 14, 2026
“We knew that it was his moment,” Tonya said. “For him to go out there, for him to decide that, ‘I’m ready,’ it took for him to trust this entire process. Trust the surgeon. Trust the surgery. Trust his workout and his recovery. He had to trust this entire journey for him to step out on that field and know that he was ready to play.”
Next week, and throughout the rest of the season, his family will be back watching.

full_text:
Devin Singletary and the Giants surprised the favored Cowboys behind a strong all-around performance on Sunday night. Elsa / Getty Images
Every week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
Week 1 was a doozy! The best team in the league — a “superteam,” or so we thought based on our initial power rankings — got hammered, a Super Bowl rematch didn’t change the result from February, at least three Super Bowl contenders opened with a loss and points were way up .
With that, the first week of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, and we finally have some meaningful results to examine. So let’s take a look in this week’s power rankings at what we learned from each team.
What we learned: The offense is still humming
After the franchise’s drama-filled offseason and with questions about the aging roster, the 49ers had no trouble moving the ball against the Rams. Brock Purdy threw for three touchdowns, the running game (including rookie Kaelon Black) looked good and Raheem Morris’ defense was great. It’d be hard to draw up a better start.
Up next: vs. Dolphins, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Beat Patriots 13-10
What we learned: That run defense is still elite
Against a Patriots team that spent its whole offseason focused on running the ball better after getting humiliated in the Super Bowl, the Seahawks’ run defense dominated once again. Seattle limited New England to 2.5 yards per attempt on its designed rushes. Plenty is still unknown about how long Sam Darnold will be out, but — no surprise — the defense is still great.
Up next: at Cardinals, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
What we learned: They’re the AFC favorites
The Bills were a trendy pick to reach the Super Bowl this season, even in their first year under new coach Joe Brady. They showed why on Sunday. The Texans might have the best defense in the NFL, yet the Bills put up 409 yards of offense while Josh Allen threw for a pair of touchdowns and added another two on the ground. That offense will be fun for the home crowd to watch as Buffalo unveils its new stadium Thursday night.
Up next: vs. Lions, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
1-0. pic.twitter.com/XguSOY6RL8
— Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 13, 2026
Sunday: Beat Panthers 59-37
What we learned: Best offense in the NFL?
Ben Johnson told our Dan Pompei this offseason that he wanted to build the highest-scoring offense in league history. It seemed outlandish at the time. Then the Bears hung 59 on the Panthers in Week 1, and suddenly anything seems possible. The defense carries plenty of questions, but that offense was unbelievable.
Up next: vs. Vikings, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
What we learned: The young OC might work
The Ravens raised some eyebrows around the league during the offseason when they hired a 29-year-old offensive coordinator. Declan Doyle is now 30, but the young coach and a healthy Lamar Jackson led to an impressive rout in Week 1 that featured 506 yards of offense.
Up next: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Thursday: Lost to 49ers 27-7
What we learned: Sleep helps
The season didn’t start well for the NFL’s superteam that has Super Bowl-or-bust aspirations. Matthew Stafford, the defending league MVP, threw for just 155 yards with no touchdowns and an interception in Australia. Now Myles Garrett is on injured reserve and out for at least four games.
Up next: vs. Giants, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Monday: Beat Broncos 31-10
What we learned: They have a running game!
After dealing with an inconsistent ground attack last season, the Chiefs went out and signed reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III. It took Walker one game to make a big impact. All eyes in the opener were on Patrick Mahomes’ return, but it was Walker who stole the show, totaling 191 yards of offense and two touchdowns, and adding a new dimension to the K.C. offense.
Up next: vs. Colts, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Saints 31-30 (OT)
What we learned: A throwing motion negates a fumble
The Lions were saved when an apparent Jared Goff fumble was ruled an incompletion thanks to a statute many had never heard of before. The Lions went on to survive a crazy second-half comeback by the Saints that exposed several significant flaws . But, hey, they’re still 1-0 entering a big Thursday night showdown.
Up next: at Bills, Thursday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Bills 36-31
What we learned: The defense is beatable
That side of the ball is supposed to carry this team. Even though the Bills had the ball for under 24 minutes of game time, the Texans’ usually dominant defense still got gashed at home. C.J. Stroud was better Sunday than in the playoffs, which is the last time we saw him, but his strip-sack in the final seconds cemented Houston’s loss.
Up next: vs. Bengals, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Wednesday: Lost to Seahawks 13-10
What we learned: Drake Maye’s slump isn’t over
The Patriots had hoped that Maye’s four-game postseason slide last season was largely the result of a shoulder injury and some big games in bad weather against great defenses. But with a full offseason to prepare, Maye struggled again against the Seahawks, throwing three interceptions, including a brutal one in the end zone when New England easily could’ve forced overtime.
Up next: vs. Steelers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Commanders 24-22
What we learned: Jalen Hurts can still produce moments
The final box score isn’t going to instill a ton of faith that the Eagles’ offense has suddenly morphed back into one of the league’s best. But Hurts made enough big plays when his team needed him, connecting on a deep ball and improvising with his legs on a third-and-18 conversion to offer hope as Philadelphia settles into this new offensive scheme under Sean Mannion.
Up next: at Titans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Monday: Lost to Chiefs 31-10
What we learned: There’s concern on offense
In a bit of a surprise this offseason, coach Sean Payton relinquished offensive play-calling duties to 31-year-old coordinator Davis Webb. His debut didn’t go well. After a pair of offseason ankle surgeries, Bo Nix fumbled three times, threw an interception and managed just 4.7 yards per attempt, while new receiver Jaylen Waddle had only one catch for 2 yards.
Up next: vs. Jaguars, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Did we really learn anything about the Jaguars by watching them beat a hapless Browns team? Still, props to them for jumping out to a 31-0 lead and putting it on cruise control behind a great game from Trevor Lawrence and an impressive showing from the defense. Now, the schedule turns brutal with five straight games against teams with Super Bowl hopes.
Up next: at Broncos, Sunday, 4:05 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Buccaneers 33-27
What we learned: They have a defense!
The bar might have been on the floor for that side of the ball after last season, but the new-look Cincinnati defense came to play against Tampa Bay, forcing four turnovers and notching four sacks. It was an especially impressive win considering Ja’Marr Chase caught only two passes for 12 yards.
Up next: at Texans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Packers 39-22
What we learned: Brian Flores is a mad man
And we mean that in a good way. The Minnesota defensive coordinator sent blitzes on 74 percent(!) of the Packers’ dropbacks and totally overwhelmed their offensive line late as the Vikings put together an impressive comeback win with backup quarterback Carson Wentz leading the offense.
Up next: at Bears, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Beat Falcons 20-13
What we learned: Things look familiar
Yes, the Steelers have a new coach, but this team looked much like it has in recent years. The defense was pretty good. The offense was mostly fine. It’s rarely worth putting too much stock into Week 1, but this Mike McCarthy-led squad looks like another roughly .500 team. We should learn more about the Steelers in Week 2 during their trip to New England.
Up next: at Patriots, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Sunday: Lost to Vikings 39-22
What we learned: New season, same Packers
That was the headline…

full_text:
Kenyon Sadiq caught all three of his targets to go with a 3-yard touchdown run on Sunday. Steve Roberts / Imagn Images
NASHVILLE — Kenyon Sadiq’s high school coach received a questionnaire last fall from an NFL team — the same team Sadiq will face in his second game as a professional football player.
The form asked variations of the same question: Where do you see him playing in the NFL?
It’s a question Scott Berger had been answering in some form for a long time. When Sadiq played in high school, he was a wide receiver.
But on that questionnaire from the Green Bay Packers last year, Berger laid out a vision for Sadiq that might as well serve as the outline for how the New York Jets are planning on — and, based on Week 1, already are — using him.
“I think he’ll be a matchup problem because he’s faster than a linebacker, and if they put one of those nickel corners on him he’s bigger and stronger than they are,” Berger said. “I just think that he’s going to be a real good move-type of guy.”
Sadiq’s first college touchdown, in the 2024 Fiesta Bowl against Liberty, came with Oregon in 14 personnel (one running back and four tight ends). When the ball was snapped, he ran behind Bo Nix, who tossed it to him, and he took it into the end zone for a 3-yard touchdown. The first teammates to greet him in the end zone were his tight end teammates, Terrance Ferguson and Patrick Herbert.
That sounds familiar if you just watched the Jets’ Week 1 victory over the Tennessee Titans on Sunday — specifically their first touchdown of the season. On their first drive, the Jets lined up in 13-personnel (three tight ends, one running back) with Sadiq positioned at almost the same exact spot he was in the Liberty Bowl on the right side. He cut behind quarterback Geno Smith, who handed him the ball. Sadiq, behind some expert blocking, coasted into the front corner of the end zone for his first NFL touchdown. The first teammates to greet him in the end zone were his tight end teammates, Mason Taylor and Jeremy Ruckert.
“I knew it was coming,” Sadiq said of the touchdown. “It was just a matter of time. It was just surreal.”
Said Smith: “I mean, that’s what we’ve seen from him. Every time he’s been on the field, whether it was in practice or even in the game, he’s a guy who’s going to make an impact. He’s a professional, he understands what to do … he showed up in a big way.”
It was the first drive of the Jets’ 2026 season and it set the tone for what was to come on Sunday. Sadiq had his first career reception earlier in the drive. All told, the first-round rookie played 28 snaps, giving a little preview of the sort of mismatch he will be, and how Frank Reich will use him to keep defenses off balance.
Sadiq represents the hope for something more on offense, something creative — something fun. Yes, this Jets offense looked fun against the Titans: a flowing passing game, a successful run game and a dominant offensive line. The Jets can finally win with some offensive creativity, and Sadiq might be the face of that.
Some evidence: The Jets ran three plays out of 13 personnel on their opening drive and 11 plays overall, per TruMedia. They only ran three plays out of that personnel all of last season. On Sunday, they also ran one play in 14 personnel and 15 in 12 personnel (one running back, two tight ends). Sadiq, with his versatility, is the key that unlocks those groupings.
As Glenn pointed out, at one point during Sunday’s game the Titans were flagged for too many men on the field because a personnel package with extra tight ends had them scrambling.
“That’s something that we’ve talked about since we drafted Sadiq, was to be able to match him up with Mason (Taylor), (Jeremy) Ruckert, and Jelani (Woods) and to be able to move these guys around because they can do so much,” Glenn said. “I thought that was pretty fun to see.”
Even after missing most of training camp because of hernia surgery, Sadiq has already shown he is the kind of athlete and versatile offensive weapon to keep defenses honest. He’s a tight end with a movable skillset that very few others at his position can match. It’s why the Jets drafted him with the 16th pick — and why other teams wanted him.
One assistant coach from a team that drafted ahead of the Jets told The Athletic on Sunday that he wished their team had drafted Sadiq.
Additionally, Berger said that when he spoke to a Los Angeles Rams scout, they told him, “Hey, we like tight ends,” Berger recalled. “We like lots of them. We like to move them around. He said that’s why we’re interested in Kenyon.”
The Jets, it turns out, feel the same way.
At the root of that is his athleticism — his speed and strength — combined with a high football IQ. “The good thing is,” Reich said, “he’s very smart.”
Former Oregon offensive coordinator Will Stein, now the head coach at Kentucky, said in the spring that he thinks Sadiq is going to be “terrorizing defenses” in the NFL in short order.
“He can be in-line, he can be off the ball, he could be in a fullback position, he’d be on the perimeter, at receiver,” Stein said. “A scout told me, I couldn’t agree more, like whatever position he’s lined up at, that’s what position he looks like he’s supposed to play. He looks natural at so many spots.”
At Oregon, Sadiq was productive last year (560 yards, eight touchdowns) but was battling injuries and was rarely at full strength even while playing most of the Ducks’ snaps. In an offense flush with talent, the Jets won’t need Sadiq to be anyone’s No. 1 or 2 target. He’s not even their No. 1 tight end — he’s behind Mason Taylor on the depth chart and rotating with both Jeremy Ruckert (29 snaps on Sunday) and Jelani Woods (16). Still, don’t be surprised if Sadiq is being talked about on a grander scale in this offense as the season progresses and he gains more experience.
One reason to feel that way: Think about how much time he missed. Sadiq played in rookie minicamp, had hernia surgery, missed all of OTAs and minicamp, returned early in training camp — long enough for the Jets to test out the end-around he scored on — but then had a setback and didn’t return to practice until just before the regular season. As a result, Reich said the Jets would likely have to throttle back their plans for Sadiq because of the time missed.
That might have been lip service. There Sadiq was on the very first drive of the season, playing a crucial role as a weapon that Reich and Smith already trust.
That trust was largely built on a belief in Sadiq’s talent and raw athleticism, sure, but also in the way he works — and has worked behind the scenes as he’s climbed back from injury.
“It just felt really good,” Sadiq said, “to get back out there.”

title: New offense, familiar problem: Why the Eagles stalled again after halftime The Eagles stalled while debuting an 'aggressive' approach under new OC Sean Mannion. What are the fixes? Brooks Kubena 20
summary:
Jalen Hurts (1) rescued the Eagles, but penalties and protection breakdowns showed how much work Sean Mannion’s new offense still needs. Michael Owens / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — There were new schemes, new coaches, but ultimately a continuation of a year-old problem.
Jalen Hurts’ second-half heroics allow new Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion to solve second-half stalls in the safety of the win column — much like his predecessor did until the stalls eventually did him in.
full_text:
Jalen Hurts (1) rescued the Eagles, but penalties and protection breakdowns showed how much work Sean Mannion’s new offense still needs. Michael Owens / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — There were new schemes, new coaches, but ultimately a continuation of a year-old problem.
Jalen Hurts’ second-half heroics allow new Philadelphia Eagles offensive coordinator Sean Mannion to solve second-half stalls in the safety of the win column — much like his predecessor did until the stalls eventually did him in.
The 2025 Eagles were the only team in coach Nick Sirianni’s tenure to finish a season with a negative second-half scoring margin (-7). The 2026 Eagles own a minus-3 second-half point differential after Week 1. Debuts offer some forgiveness. So do wins . Mannion, a first-time play caller, will look back on a mostly brutal 20-play sequence that portrayed the antithesis of the “aggressive” approach Sirianni said they’d intended entering the second half.
“We don’t think about taking our foot off the gas,” Sirianni said afterward.
Not intentionally. Not unless they’re bleeding the clock while nursing a lead with four minutes left in the game. But the Eagles went three-and-out on their first three drives of the second half. Several offensive players said Mannion wanted to turn to their wide zone run game after establishing a 14-9 halftime lead. The Washington Commanders thwarted the plan by sending preemptive pressure against offensive looks with a small sample of tendencies.
The Eagles opened the second half with Hurts under center in 12 personnel. They had used the same two-tight-end presentation five times on first downs in the first half — and ran the ball on four of those occasions. The Commanders blitzed both cornerbacks and trapped Saquon Barkley for a one-yard loss. The blitz package suited the arrangement of tight ends Dallas Goedert and Johnny Mundt, who bracketed the offensive line.
To open the next drive, Hurts dropped back in the same look, but Goedert and Mundt lined up on the left. The Commanders blitzed linebacker Sonny Styles on the weak side, and Styles bowled over Barkley to sack Hurts for a 6-yard loss.
Mannion appeared to try to manufacture some aid for the Eagles’ wide zone runs on the third drive. Mundt motioned rightward to clear more runway for Barkley on a second-and-7 run. But Styles blitzed through the same gap as before (and what had previously been the weak side) and burst past right guard Tyler Steen and right tackle Lane Johnson before tackling Barkley for a 3-yard loss.
“There was some exotic stuff,” Mundt said of the blitzes. “You can talk about it all you want on a whiteboard, and then you see it when the bullets are flying and it’s a different story.”
The wide zone concept is central to Mannion’s offense. It fits within the philosophy the Eagles are trying to enforce. They aim to be the aggressor by getting calls in quickly, getting promptly to the line and running their plays while playing less pre-snap chess.
Instead, the Eagles were again beneficiaries of a defense that forced three-and-outs at a 45.4 percent clip (up from 27.8 percent in 2025) and a career day from punter Braden Mann (who twice pinned punts within the 10, once within the 5). Players blamed poor execution for putting Hurts in situations such as the third-and-18 he converted with a 22-yard scramble in the fourth quarter.
“We’ve got to help (Mannion) out,” Hurts said. “We should never be in third-and-18. We should never be in that position.”
The Eagles totaled three holding penalties — all on first down. (Their most first-down holds since a Week 5 win over the Arizona Cardinals in 2022.) Aside from sacks, they totaled four negative plays — three on first down (doubling their average in 2025). Hurts was sacked three times and threw four passes away while either getting hit or evading pressure. The setbacks contributed to the Eagles’ highest second-down average distance to the sticks (9.9 yards) in the Sirianni era, per TruMedia.
“We can’t shoot ourselves in the foot,” said center Cam Jurgens, who was twice flagged for holding.
Hurts was pressured on 35.7 percent of his dropbacks. Left guard Landon Dickerson was responsible for many of the pressures, including Commanders linebacker Frankie Luvu’s punt-forcing sack in the first quarter. Dickerson said he was playing through bone bruising in his right knee that he suffered in practice “a few weeks ago.” He acknowledged that he “played like s—,” but ultimately was restricted by the injury. The Eagles are placing Dickerson on injured reserve with the intention of bringing him back for the stretch run of the season.
His absence will test the Eagles’ interior offensive line depth. General manager Howie Roseman closed training camp by telling reporters that if any of them had given him truth serum and said, “What are you looking for in training camp?”, it would have been how their interior offensive line depth panned out. It stands to reason that Roseman shared that insight because of the progress Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin showed throughout the preseason.
Beyond the offensive line play, Hurts cited moments in which the Eagles beat themselves with their lack of pace. He took ownership for not generating more urgency after his 64-yard bomb to Tay Wicks in the first quarter. The Eagles did not get set quickly enough at the Commanders’ 6, forcing Sirianni to burn a timeout with one second left on the play clock.
In 2025, the Eagles led the NFL with 150 plays with one second left on the play clock . Against Washington, the Eagles averaged 1.4 yards on five plays snapped with one second left on the play clock until Hurts’ decisive 43-yard touchdown pass to Goedert in the fourth quarter — a play Goedert acknowledged was a happy accident.
Goedert said they had two plays in the huddle. The Eagles led 17-16 while facing a third-and-6 situation with 6:12 left in the game. Goedert said Hurts “killed” one play just before the snap. Goedert slid laterally, responding to the call, but did not draw an illegal shift penalty because his lateral movement fell within the rules.
Styles, calling for a flag, lagged behind Goedert’s route. Hurts hit Goedert in the middle of the field, and Goedert, sensing from the corner of his eye that safety Nick Cross was overplaying in pursuit, pirouetted to the left and swerved upfield for the score.
“It was so funny,” Mundt said. “We were looking at the iPad after, when it was right before he caught the ball. And there was like three defenders. And (reserve tight end) Grant (Calcaterra) was like, ‘Score, or no score?’ And 99 percent of people would say, ‘No score,’ just based on angles and stuff. And the move he made, that was killer. That was awesome.”
I asked Johnny Mundt about Dallas Goedert's 43-yard touchdown reception, when Goedert cleverly curled back toward the sideline to break free.
"It was so funny," Mundt said. "We were looking at the iPad after, when it was right before he caught the ball. And there was like three… pic.twitter.com/aWATQJy1J4
— Brooks Kubena (@BKubena) September 14, 2026
The Eagles know transcending the system with talent alone isn’t sustainable. The 2025 Eagles are one of 11 teams out of 70 that made the playoffs since 2021 despite a negative second-half point differential. No such team has reached the Super Bowl since at least 2000.
One game doesn’t suggest a trend, and one week isn’t enough to judge Mannion’s system. But the Eagles put plenty of plays on film that curbed a style of play in which they are supposed to be the aggressor.
The early-down issues forced Mannion to adjust his calls. Hence, a new collection of offensive players still doesn’t quite know the rhythm of their play caller — or which concepts or packages he favors.
Asked Friday whether taking regular vertical shots was still a big part of this year’s passing game, DeVonta Smith said, “I don’t know the flow of how Sean calls games.” Sunday’s negative plays skewed further deductions.

title: Five ways Mike McCarthy and a new coaching staff changed the Steelers in Week 1 On both sides of the ball, the Steelers took a much different approach in their Week 1 win over the Falcons. Mike DeFabo 14
summary:
On Sunday, Mike McCarthy's offense attacked downfield much more frequently than the Steelers did a year ago. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
A new era of Steelers football began on Sunday with a 20-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons. While it may have felt familiar to see a third-string quarterback hang around until T.J. Watt produced a game-breaking moment, you don’t have to look far below the surface to see the ways in which the new staff will put its fingerprint on the team.
The personnel deployment,
full_text:
On Sunday, Mike McCarthy's offense attacked downfield much more frequently than the Steelers did a year ago. Joe Sargent / Getty Images
A new era of Steelers football began on Sunday with a 20-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons. While it may have felt familiar to see a third-string quarterback hang around until T.J. Watt produced a game-breaking moment, you don’t have to look far below the surface to see the ways in which the new staff will put its fingerprint on the team.
The personnel deployment, schematics and big-picture approach to risk all shifted. Let’s dive deeper.
Mike McCarthy might be 62 years old, but he’s not old-school. He often talks about analytics, GPS monitoring and sports science guiding his decision-making. Before each game, McCarthy’s staff puts together a playing-time projection report. The idea is to keep players fresh deeper into games and also deeper into seasons.
“As a head coach, you have to look at all the snaps over the course of the season,” McCarthy said. “How many quality rushes do your outside pieces have? I mean, is it 20? Is it 25? Whatever that number is, you have to factor that in because when the game’s on the line or there’s important parts in the game, you want those guys to be fresh and ready to go.”
Watt certainly was fresh early in the fourth quarter when he logged a sack, a tackle for loss and then the pick-six quick succession. That’s all part of a calculated plan. Last season, Watt played more than 60 snaps in seven games, including a season-high 70 snaps in Week 14. On Sunday, that number dipped to 37.
That’s his lowest snap count since Week 18 of the 2023 season, when he played 30 snaps and left the game in the third quarter with a knee injury. To put that further in perspective, when Watt was on a “pitch count” on his first game back from a punctured lung last year, the Steelers played him 42 plays.
Given the depth of the outside linebacker room and Watt’s age (he turns 32 in October), it makes even more sense to split up the reps. Alex Highsmith played 40 snaps, Nick Herbig played 37 and Jack Sawyer played 21.
“With the rotation we have, getting less reps, I was trying to exert as much as you possibly can on those reps, making them mean that much more,” Watt said.
Last season, the Steelers allowed a league-worst 10.2 points per game in the fourth quarter. In the short term, maybe keeping Watt and others fresh deeper into games can help them reverse this stat. Longer term, it makes sense to take a calculated approach to player usage with a team that’s one of the league’s oldest, especially at some of the most critical positions.
A year ago at this time, coach Mike Tomlin was boasting that Darius Slay, Joey Porter Jr. and Jalen Ramsey would give the Steelers a chance to play man coverage against any team in the league. During Patrick Graham’s debut, the new defensive coordinator didn’t run any pure man coverages, according to Pro Football Focus. Instead, the Steelers ran Cover 3 on 43.9 percent of snaps, Quarters on 29.8 percent and Cover 6 on 22.8 percent. That’s about as dramatic a shift as possible.
“I’ve told you guys before, my philosophy is what’s best for that week usually,” Graham said. “We’ve got guys that can play man, guys that can play zone.”
It would be easy to say the Steelers were missing Joey Porter Jr. , their top man corner, so they leaned into zones. Maybe that’s true to a degree. But the change also shows how Graham is updating a defense that has long needed modernization.
In all four of Teryl Austin’s seasons as defensive coordinator, Pittsburgh ran man coverage on 30 percent of snaps or more, including 31.1 percent of snaps in 2025 (fourth-most). Over that same span from 2022 to 2025, the Raiders ranked 20th overall with 22.5 percent man coverage usage. Last year, the Raiders ran man coverage on 14.6 percent of snaps, the third-lowest rate in the league, according to Pro Football Focus.
This suggests Graham’s decision to play more zone coverage should be a trend that continues this season. It’s also the way the league is moving, as modern offenses full of pre-snap motions and shifts can expose man coverages.
The other part of this conversation is how the Steelers are updating their zone coverages.
“The beautiful thing now (with) zone coverage, you have an element of man on a side a lot of times anyway,” Graham said. “You have three deep (Cover 3), and the backside could be manned up. You have quarters, and I mean …”
Graham trailed off but his point was quarters coverage often has a match element built into it. To put it in the most basic terms, there are two types of zone: spot drop and pattern match. In spot drop, players are responsible for one specific area on the field. In pattern match, the assignment can change based on the formation and route concepts. As the play unfolds, what can start as zone can end up playing out like man.
“They don’t talk about us being as evolved as the offenses, but we we have some things up our sleeve too,” Graham said. “What you might perceive is zone, or whoever is looking at it might be zone, but there might be a sprinkle of man in there.”
The Steelers’ offensive formula last year was to get the ball out of Aaron Rodgers’ hand faster than anyone else and throw it shorter than anyone else. This approach asked Rogers to be near-perfect during long, sustained scoring drives, while also leaning heavily into yards after the catch.
Given the QB is still the same and some of those tactics are part of the West Coast approach, we’ll likely still see some of that from the Steelers’ offense. However, there was a much more concerted effort to push the ball downfield Sunday.
Last year, Rodgers’ air yards per attempt sat at 5.9. He boosted that to 8.8 in Week 1. Last season, Rodgers attempted passes with 15-plus air yards on 16.3 percent of his throws. That number more than doubled to 34.3 percent in Week 1.
Now, the execution on those plays needs to improve; the Steelers have acknowledged that. But there should be a greater emphasis on throwing over the middle and deeper.
Related to the outside-linebacker rotation was the deployment of Herbig. After signing a four-year, $100 million extension, he’ll need to be a bigger part of the game plan — and he was Sunday. At times, Herbig rushed off the edge in a traditional way. Other times, he was playing on the interior in packages with three outside linebackers on the field together. But perhaps the most interesting deployment was when the Steelers aligned Herbig off the ball behind a four-down front.
“It starts with his athleticism,” Graham said. “He could do a lot of things, from playing on the edge, playing in space. He’s an athletic football player. Then you go to his intelligence. What he can handle?
“As a play caller, I look at the field as a grid. I’m trying to figure out how to weaponize these guys and try to get them more involved.”
The anticipated shift from a tight end-centric offense to a wide receiver-friendly one occurred Sunday. Last year, Steelers ran 11 personnel (one back, one tight end, three receivers) on 38.7 percent of snaps. That was the second-lowest rate in the league. As anticipated, McCarthy’s offense featured three receivers much more frequently. The Steelers ran 11 personnel on 57.8 percent of snaps (an increase of about 20 percentage points compared to last year).
The fullback is also not dead in Pittsburgh. The Steelers ran plays with two backs in the backfield 7.8 percent of the time. That number could continue to grow as the staff gains more faith in rookie fullback Riley Nowakoski.

title: What do the 49ers do after De'Zhaun Stribling's and Alfred Collins' injuries? Mailbag Among this week's questions: Who fills in for Stribling, and will Ricky Pearsall's injury add an extra year to his rookie contract? Matt Barrows 13
summary:
De'Zhaun Stribling was much more than a slot receiver before he was injured in the season opener. Robert Cianflone / Getty Images
The San Francisco 49ers looked strong on Thursday. But how do they become stronger?
That’s the question on everyone’s mind this week after the team lost a defensive tackle, Alfred Collins, for the season and a wide receiver, De’Zhaun Stribling, for an undetermined amount of time. Will the 49ers add a receiver? And which defensive linemen are available after serious in
full_text:
De'Zhaun Stribling was much more than a slot receiver before he was injured in the season opener. Robert Cianflone / Getty Images
The San Francisco 49ers looked strong on Thursday. But how do they become stronger?
That’s the question on everyone’s mind this week after the team lost a defensive tackle, Alfred Collins, for the season and a wide receiver, De’Zhaun Stribling, for an undetermined amount of time. Will the 49ers add a receiver? And which defensive linemen are available after serious injuries to Collins and Sam Okuayinonu?
We answer these questions and more in this week’s mailbag. Thanks for all the great queries, which, as usual, have been lightly edited for length and clarity.
What happens at slot receiver while Stribling is out? — Bryan C.
One of the bigger surprises from the game was that Stribling wasn’t just a slot receiver. He was a starting receiver. Of the 21 snaps he took before leaving the game with an ankle injury — the most snaps of any 49ers receiver to that point — only five came out of the slot, with the other 16 outside.
As noted in this week’s minutia minute , Mike Evans worked out of the slot to begin the game, with his first three catches — all third-down conversions — coming when he was in the slot. Here’s how the slot snaps stacked up on Thursday:
All of which is to say that the 49ers have a lot of options and were already rotating a lot in the slot before Stribling was injured.
Do you see Deebo Samuel’s playing time and role expanding, or do they keep Demarcus Robinson at the Z and keep Deebo fresh on limited plays again? — Ezra M.
I think both players’ snap counts will rise as a result of Stribling’s injury, but perhaps Robinson’s will rise more.
Keeping Samuel fresh seems like the right idea. For example, his kickoff return to begin the second half Thursday hasn’t gotten enough attention. That was a big play for a team that badly wanted to send a message at the start of the third quarter. Samuel might be more effective occasionally being featured on plays than he would if he were a nearly every-down receiver.
As for Robinson, he and Purdy seem to have a good connection. Last year was a strange one for Robinson. He appeared to develop a rapport with Purdy during training camp. But then he had to sit out the first three games due to a suspension, and when he came back, Purdy was injured. Robinson didn’t seem to have the same chemistry with Mac Jones (whose rapport was with Kendrick Bourne instead), and it wasn’t until Purdy was back and feeling like himself late in the season that Robinson became a real factor.
With the injury to Stribling, do you think the 49ers are now in the market for a WR? — Brandon A.
No, I don’t think so. They can promote KhaDarel Hodge from the practice squad. And they can activate Christian Kirk from injured reserve after Week 4.
With tight end Jake Tonges (knee) apparently out for a while, do you see the 49ers going for a street signing, or will they go with their internal options? — Alberto R.
I see them going with an internal option. They’ll probably promote Brayden Willis, who made the initial 53-man roster, from the practice squad. Practice squadder Khalil Dinkins, an undrafted rookie, is also a possibility. However, he joined training camp late and might be a better option deeper into the season.
So obviously the 49ers are going to win the Super Bowl. To temper our enthusiasm, what things from the game would you say stood out as areas of concern despite the big win? — Jason H.
There were more injuries. And a defense that finished with a league-low 20 sacks last season had zero on Thursday.
Which free-agent defensive tackle and/or defensive end could they sign as a decent depth piece with some upside? — Marco S.
I know they just lost Collins , a starter at defensive tackle. But I still think the bigger need is at defensive end.
Though Mykel Williams is technically a defensive end, he’ll be able to play a lot of defensive tackle snaps — especially on obvious passing downs — when he’s back after Week 4. The same goes for Keion White.
There are also a lot more quality defensive ends available, a list that includes Haason Reddick, Leonard Floyd and Joey Bosa. Here’s how I’d classify them:
• If the team wants another Romello Height-like player or is worried it’s not getting enough out of Height, Reddick would be a good solution. He’s a lighter-bodied edge player who’s played in systems similar to the one defensive coordinator Raheem Morris is running this year.
• If the team wants a dependable, every-down defensive end, Floyd is the answer. He’s familiar to both the 49ers’ brass and Morris. Yes, Floyd turned 34 last week and had only 3.5 sacks last year for Morris’ Falcons. But the 49ers aren’t in a position to look down their noses at 3.5 sacks. Their sack leader last year had four.
• If the 49ers want a second-half-of-the-season boost, how about Bosa? The team might be worried about how Nick Bosa’s oft-injured older brother might hold up over a 17-game season. But an eight-game season seems reasonable. Joey had five sacks and 54 quarterback pressures for the Bills last year. That’s not elite, but it’s better than what the 49ers have opposite Nick at the moment.
Another interesting option is Yetur Gross-Matos, whose recent stint with the 49ers was marred by a knee issue. Gross-Matos didn’t play or practice much, but when he was on the field, he made an impact. His 16.3 percent pass-rush win rate last season was second best on the team behind Bosa’s 20 percent rate.
Gross-Matos is currently rehabilitating from that knee injury and isn’t ready to play. That could change by midseason.
After one game … early choice for rookie who makes the biggest impact this year? My vote is Gracen Halton. — Rob C.
There seem to be several good choices, including Halton, Kaelon Black, Jaden Dugger and, depending on how much time he misses, Stribling.
I’ll go with Dugger. He played more than half the defensive snaps and spent a lot of time rushing the quarterback against the Rams. He seemed a touch tentative on Thursday, which ought to disappear the more he plays.
Do you see Malik Mustapha splitting time with Ji’Ayir Brown or riding the bench this season? Brown is an expensive free agent in 2027. — David L.
The 49ers never dole out big money for safeties — ironic given who their general manager is — so it’s hard to see them bringing back Brown for big money, whether he’s a 17-game starter this season or not.
I don’t think he gets the hook yet. But the 49ers had no issues rotating the safeties last year, and they had one of their best games at the position, the wild-card win in Philadelphia, with Mustapha and Marques Sigle in the lineup.
Lots of online talk about the “banana motion” from the Niners in Australia. Is that something the NFL could consider and outlaw/tell officials to clamp down on midseason? — Danny J.
An opposing coach could pull the officials aside before the game and ask them to keep an eye on the motion. But there’s nothing illegal about it unless Juszczyk is clearly moving closer to the line of scrimmage at the snap. During his banana motions on Thursday, he seemed to be just coming out of his turn at the snap.
With Ricky Pearsall missing the entire year on IR, how does that affect his rookie contract? I keep hearing that because he will miss the entire season, the 49ers get an extra year tacked onto his rookie contract. Is that true? — Jeff E.
No. Sometimes an injury will cause a player’s contract to toll — pause and extend for another year — but that happens only if he lands on the non-football injury list (meaning he was injured away from team activities) and misses the final year of his contract. Pearsall is in the third year of a four-year rookie contract and is on injured reserve, not the NFI list.
Very curious about two things: How is your personal jet lag (obvious insight into how the Niners might be feeling)? And how big of a deal is it that Kaelon Black looked so good and they…
